## The 1912 Block in Nanjing

The **1912 block** (or 1912 JieQu) is a historic neighborhood in **Nanjing**, Jiangsu Province, China. Named after the year the Republic of China was established (1912), this area near the former Presidential Palace has become renowned today as a bustling nightlife and bar district.

The Yongle Emperor (Ming Dynasty's third emperor, Zhu Di, r. 1402-1424) met with **Japanese envoys** in Nanjing in 1403-1405. So while the 1912 block in Nanjing serves as the reference point, **Sanlitun and surrounding areas in Beijing** represent some of the largest concentrations of bars in China outside of that Nanjing district.

# Yongle
## Youth and early career
The young new emperor Zhu Yunwen (the Jianwen emperor) had other intentions. Influenced by Confucian scholar-officials, he instituted a series of reforms unsettling to the newly stabilized government. One of his major goals was to take regional power away from the princes, and in 1398–99 one prince after another was imprisoned, exiled, or driven to suicide. Thus the prince of Yan found himself steadily more isolated and endangered, and in August 1399 he rose in rebellion, declaring it his avuncular duty to rescue the inexperienced emperor from his malicious advisers.

The rebellion lasted from 1399 into 1402 and devastated much of western Shandong province and the northern part of the Huai River basin. The central government at Nanjing seems to have underestimated the prince of Yan’s strength and failed to muster its manpower and matériel effectively; the war was a long stalemate. In early 1402 the prince of Yan’s forces broke through the imperial armies in the north, sped almost unopposed southward along the Grand Canal, accepted surrender of the imperial fleet on the Yangtze River, and were admitted into the walled capital by court defectors in July 1402. Four days after the fall of Nanjing, the prince of Yan took the throne himself, although he did not formally begin his rule until 1403; he took the reign name Yongle (“Perpetual Happiness”). The Jianwen emperor had disappeared. Whether he died in a palace fire (as was officially announced) or escaped in disguise to live many more years as a recluse is a puzzle that troubled Zhu Di until his own death and has been a subject of conjecture by Chinese historians ever since.

# Accession to the throne of Yongle
The accession brought terrible retribution to those who had most closely advised Jianwen. They and all their relatives were put to death. Before the purge ended, thousands had perished. The new emperor also revoked the institutional and policy changes of his nephew-predecessor and even ordered history rewritten so that the founding emperor’s era name was extended through 1402, as if the Jianwen emperor had never reigned at all. The one reform policy that remained in effect was that princely powers must be curtailed. Hence, the surviving frontier princes were successively transferred from their strategically located fiefs into central and south China and were deprived of all governmental authority. From the Yongle period on, imperial princes were no more than salaried idlers who socially and ceremonially adorned the cities to which they were assigned and in which they were effectively confined. No subsequent Ming emperor was seriously threatened by a princely uprising.
As the Yongle emperor, Zhu Di was domineering, jealous of his authority, and inclined toward self-aggrandizement. He staffed the central government with young men dependent on himself and relied to an unprecedented extent on eunuchs for service outside their traditionally prescribed palace spheres—as foreign envoys, as supervisors of special projects such as the requisitioning of construction supplies, and as regional overseers of military garrisons. In 1420 he established a special eunuch agency called the Eastern Depot (Dongchang) charged with ferreting out treasonable activities. Although it did not become notorious in his own reign, it came to be a hated and feared secret police in collaboration with the imperial bodyguard in later decades and centuries.
The Yongle emperor also relied heavily on a secretarial group of young scholar-officials assigned to palace duty from the traditional compiling and editing agency, the Hanlin Academy, and by the end of his reign they became a Grand Secretariat, a powerful buffer between the emperor and the administrative agencies of government. Although the emperor, like his father, was quick to anger and sometimes abused officials cruelly, he built a strong and effective administration, and during his reign China settled into the generally stable political and socioeconomic patterns that were to characterize the remainder of the dynasty.

# Accession to the throne of Yongle
Like his father, Yongle had little personal respect for the higher forms of Chinese culture. In the fashion of the Mongol khans, he summoned to China and highly honoured a Tibetan lama, and the strongest intellectual influence on him may have been that of a monk named Daoyan, a long-favoured personal adviser. Along more orthodox lines, his government sponsored the compilation and publication of Confucian and Neo-Confucian Classics, and it most notably sponsored the preparation in manuscript form of a monumental compendium of literature called _Yongle dadian_ (“The Great Canon of the Yongle Era”) in more than 11,000 volumes, which preserved many works that would otherwise have been lost. But the emperor himself must have considered such activities a kind of busywork for litterateurs who enjoyed public esteem but not his personal trust. A military man of action, the Yongle emperor had little enough patience with unavoidable administrative business, much less with intellectual exercises.

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Mongolian campaigns
The balance of power on the steppe shifted after 1410. In 1412, the Oirat leader Mahmud killed Bunyashiri and established a puppet khan at Karakorum. As he expanded eastward against Arughtai in an apparent attempt to unite the Mongols under his rule, the Oirats emerged as a powerful new force. Their rise alarmed the Ming court and prompted the Yongle Emperor to launch a second campaign into Mongolia in 1414.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988226-154) The Oirat cavalry suffered heavy losses in a battle along the upper Tuul River due to the superior firepower of the Ming artillery. By August, the Emperor was content with the situation and returned to Beijing.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988227-157)
Renewed hostilities erupted in 1421 when the Eastern Mongols launched cross-border raids. The Emperor decided to march against them in 1422, 1423, and 1424 despite opposition from his ministers. His efforts were ultimately unsuccessful. The campaign was costly and achieved few tangible results, largely because the Mongols avoided direct confrontation with the advancing Ming armies.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988227%E2%80%93228-158) The Emperor died while returning from his fifth campaign in Mongolia.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988228-159)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Mongolian campaigns
The Emperor had been unable to subdue the Mongols. His campaigns into Mongolia did not result in any lasting changes and proved to be extremely costly.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988228-159) Although the Chinese had larger armies, more resources, and better weaponry, the nomads' mobility and the vastness of the battlefield negated these advantages.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWang2011113-160) The Yongle Emperor's policy of exploiting divisions among rival Mongol leaders also proved unsuccessful. Rather than securing Ming influence, it alienated the competing factions and undermined relations between the Mongols and the Ming dynasty. His policies, particularly the withdrawal of several forward garrisons to the vicinity of the Great Wall, weakened the Ming dynasty's position in the steppe.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988228-159)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
[edit]
Among the Jurchens living in Manchuria, the Ming government sought to maintain peace along the frontier and counter Korean influence. It also aimed to obtain horses and other local products, such as furs, while promoting Chinese culture and values among the Jurchens.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988266%E2%80%93267-161) The Yongle Emperor sent the first mission to Manchuria in 1403, offering Chinese goods and titles in exchange for the Jurchens' recognition of their subordination.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988267-162) From 1411 onwards, the Emperor entrusted the eunuch Yishiha with expeditions to the distant hunting tribes of northern Manchuria.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988267-162) Yishiha's squadron sailed down the Amur River, reaching as far as its mouth at Tyr, and declared the local Jurchens as subjects of the Ming dynasty.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTELevathes1994124%E2%80%93126-163)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
By acknowledging Ming supremacy, the Koreans secured protection against northern tribes, especially the Jurchens, which brought border stability and enhanced the authority of their government through official recognition from China. The ruling Joseon dynasty only came into power in 1392.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-164) The exchange of envoys, which had been frequent under previous emperors, continued during the Yongle Emperor's reign. The Emperor's first ambassadors went to Korea in 1402 to announce his ascension. In the years that followed, there were regular contacts between the two countries, with the Koreans sending two to three delegations per year. The Koreans saw some of the Ming demands as excessive and difficult, but they fulfilled them nonetheless. These demands included providing horses and oxen for military purposes,[[xxix]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-165) bronze Buddha statues, relics, paper for printing Buddhist literature, and even sending girls to serve in the imperial harem.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-164)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
Relations with the Ashikaga government of Japan were at a standstill during the Hongwu era. Hu Weiyong, who was executed in 1380, was accused of conspiring with Japanese assistance.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-166) In 1399, Shōgun Yoshimitsu (r.1369–1408) took the initiative to restore contacts in order to make profit from trade with China.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-167) This led to another mission being sent in 1403, during which the Yongle Emperor's sovereignty was recognized. In the same year, the Ming government opened maritime trade offices in Ningbo, Quanzhou, and Guangzhou, which allowed Japanese merchants with government licenses to trade. In 1411, Shōgun Yoshimochi (r.1408–1428) implemented an isolationist policy and interrupted official relations. He also rejected the Ming's attempt to re-establish relations in 1417,[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-166) although strong demand for Chinese goods and coins sustained illegal private trade through the ports of southern Japan.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-167)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-166)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
Đại Việt faced growing internal strife by the late 14th century. The kingdom, located in present-day northern Vietnam, was known to the Ming as Annam and ruled by the Trần dynasty. Lê Quý Ly overthrew the Trần dynasty in 1400 and renamed the state Đại Ngu. The Yongle Emperor recognized the new Viet government and confirmed Lê Quý Ly's son as the ruler of Đại Ngu in the winter of 1403, but relations between the two countries were strained due to escalating border disputes. Lê Quý Ly prepared for the impending conflict and continued to engage in border skirmishes. In the spring of 1406, his soldiers ambushed Ming diplomatic envoys accompanying the Trần pretender.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTETsai2002179-168) The incident prompted the Yongle Emperor to order an invasion. The Ming army had attacked Đại Ngu from two directions by late 1406, and resistance was quelled by mid-1407. In July, the country was officially annexed to the Ming dynasty as Jiaozhi Province.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988230-169)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
Supporters of the Trần dynasty launched a rebellion in 1408, but the Ming army defeated them the next year.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988231-170) Another rebellion erupted shortly after and was only fully crushed in 1414 when the Chinese captured the rebel leader, Trần Quý Khoáng. The majority of the Ming army was unable to withdraw until 1416.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988231-170) By the end of 1417, the Viet people launched another rebellion,[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWade200680-171) led by military leader Lê Lợi. The Ming generals were unable to suppress the rebellion until the end of the Yongle Emperor's reign.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTETsai2002184%E2%80%93186-172)[[xxx]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-175)
A life-size model of one of the "medium-sized" treasure ships, measuring 63.25 meters in length, is on display at the historic Nanjing Treasure Shipyard, but there is still ongoing debate about the exact size of these treasure ships.
The giraffe, brought from Bengal in 1414, was depicted by Shen Du. The Chinese associated giraffes with the mythical creature _Qilin_.

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
In 1405, the Yongle Emperor appointed his favorite commander, the eunuch Zheng He, as admiral of a fleet with the purpose of expanding China's influence and collecting tribute from various nations. Two thousand ships were constructed to aid Zheng He in his seven voyages, including numerous large "treasure ships",[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFairbankGoldman2006137-176)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChurch2005155%E2%80%93176-177) and he embarked on six voyages to the Indian Ocean from 1405 to 1421. The first voyage took place from 1405 to 1407 and consisted of 250[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDreyer200751,_123-178) or 317[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFairbankGoldman2006137%E2%80%93138-179)[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTELevathes199482-180) ships, including 62 large "treasure ships".[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDreyer200751,_123-178) A total of 27,800 people were on board.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTETsai2002203-181) The final voyage was made during the Xuande Emperor's reign from 1431 to 1433.

The Yongle Emperor (reigned 1402 to 1424) was the third, and most famous, ruler of the Ming dynasty. It was he who sent out the huge treasure fleets which sailed into the Indian Ocean and then onward as far as Africa. It was also he who constructed the great palace complex known as the Forbidden City, in Beijing.
Explore History

#### Prince of Yan
He was born with the name Zhu Di, in 1360, the fourth son the Hongwu emperor, the founder of the Ming dynasty. While still a child he was given the title Prince of Yan. At the age of 20 he was sent to live in Beijing and given responsibility for the defence of the north-eastern sector of the Great Wall of China There, he gained experience in military affairs, and proved himself an able soldier and strategist.

#### Rebellion
When the Hongwu emperor died in 1398, the son of Zhu Di’s eldest brother came to the throne as the Jianwen emperor. Soon, the new emperor began to seek to reduce the power of his uncles, and amongst other measures summoned Zhu Di to the capital, Nanjing. Fearing that if he obeyed the summons, he would be executed, Zhu Di rebelled. In the fierce civil war that followed, Zhu Di was victorious, and succeeded in seizing the throne in 1402. He adopted the title Yongle, which means “Perpetual Happiness.”
The Yongle Emperor

#### A new capital
The Yongle Emperor immediately moved the capital from Nanjing (which means “Southern Capital”) to his former base, Beijing (“Northern Capital”). This made strategic sense as it enabled the emperor to have a huge body of troops under his direct command, stationed near the most threatened border of the empire. He personally led several expeditions into the steppes against the Mongols.
Explore History
On the other hand, Beijing was so near the border that it was vulnerable to Mongol attack. The Mongols had, until recently, ruled China and had ambitions to do so again. As Beijing was so far from the more productive parts of the empire (to the south in the Yangtze region), keeping the capital and its large garrison provisioned was hugely expensive. This became a large burden on the Ming state, and involved the refurbishment of the Grand Canal to enable it to carry the vast number of grain transports needed to feed the capital.

#### The Forbidden City
The Yongle Emperor then ordered the construction of the enormous palace complex, set within its own walls and in which the emperor’s family, his harem and his personal staff (the palace eunuchs), were largely secluded from the outside world.
This palace complex became known as the Forbidden City, and was the centre of power of the Ming Dynasty and its successor, the Qing (Manchu) Dynasty. It remains an iconic structure to this day, being a UNESCO heritage site. (Creative Commons Licence)
Explore History

#### The Treasure Fleets
Yongle is most famous for launching seven great naval expeditions “to the Western Ocean” – i.e. the Indian Ocean. He placed one his favourite palace eunuchs, Zheng He, in command of the huge fleets which sailed to Southeast Asia, India, the Persian Gulf, and the East African coast.
These fleets included the treasure ships, which were probably some of the largest sailing vassals ever built. These voyages aimed to display China’s wealth and power, establish tributary relationships with far distant lands, and secure favourable trade relations, expanding China’s influence across Asia and the Indian Ocean.

#### The Yongle Encyclopedia
As well as his more active actions, the Yongle Emperor was also interested in promoting knowledge. He therefore commissioned the _Yongle Encyclopedia_. This was the largest Chinese encyclopedia to be completed in pre-modern times, and attempted to be a compilation of all Chinese knowledge.
Explore History
Yongle died in 1424 while returning from a campaign against the Mongols. His achievements mark him as one of the most consequential of all Chinese emperors.

# Accession to the throne of Yongle
The accession brought terrible retribution to those who had most closely advised Jianwen. They and all their relatives were put to death. Before the purge ended, thousands had perished. Hence, the surviving frontier princes were successively transferred from their strategically located fiefs into central and south China and were deprived of all governmental authority. From the Yongle period on, imperial princes were no more than salaried idlers who socially and ceremonially adorned the cities to which they were assigned and in which they were effectively confined. No subsequent Ming emperor was seriously threatened by a princely uprising.
As the Yongle emperor, Zhu Di was domineering, jealous of his authority, and inclined toward self-aggrandizement. Although the emperor, like his father, was quick to anger and sometimes abused officials cruelly, he built a strong and effective administration, and during his reign China settled into the generally stable political and socioeconomic patterns that were to characterize the remainder of the dynasty.

# Accession to the throne of Yongle
Like his father, Yongle had little personal respect for the higher forms of Chinese culture. In the fashion of the Mongol khans, he summoned to China and highly honoured a Tibetan lama, and the strongest intellectual influence on him may have been that of a monk named Daoyan, a long-favoured personal adviser. Along more orthodox lines, his government sponsored the compilation and publication of Confucian and Neo-Confucian Classics, and it most notably sponsored the preparation in manuscript form of a monumental compendium of literature called _Yongle dadian_ (“The Great Canon of the Yongle Era”) in more than 11,000 volumes, which preserved many works that would otherwise have been lost. But the emperor himself must have considered such activities a kind of busywork for litterateurs who enjoyed public esteem but not his personal trust. A military man of action, the Yongle emperor had little enough patience with unavoidable administrative business, much less with intellectual exercises.

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Mongolian campaigns
The balance of power on the steppe shifted after 1410. In 1412, the Oirat leader Mahmud killed Bunyashiri and established a puppet khan at Karakorum. As he expanded eastward against Arughtai in an apparent attempt to unite the Mongols under his rule, the Oirats emerged as a powerful new force. Their rise alarmed the Ming court and prompted the Yongle Emperor to launch a second campaign into Mongolia in 1414.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988226-154) The Oirat cavalry suffered heavy losses in a battle along the upper Tuul River due to the superior firepower of the Ming artillery. By August, the Emperor was content with the situation and returned to Beijing.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988227-157)
Renewed hostilities erupted in 1421 when the Eastern Mongols launched cross-border raids. The Emperor decided to march against them in 1422, 1423, and 1424 despite opposition from his ministers. His efforts were ultimately unsuccessful. The campaign was costly and achieved few tangible results, largely because the Mongols avoided direct confrontation with the advancing Ming armies.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988227%E2%80%93228-158) The Emperor died while returning from his fifth campaign in Mongolia.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988228-159)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Mongolian campaigns
The Emperor had been unable to subdue the Mongols. His campaigns into Mongolia did not result in any lasting changes and proved to be extremely costly.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988228-159) Although the Chinese had larger armies, more resources, and better weaponry, the nomads' mobility and the vastness of the battlefield negated these advantages.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWang2011113-160) The Yongle Emperor's policy of exploiting divisions among rival Mongol leaders also proved unsuccessful. Rather than securing Ming influence, it alienated the competing factions and undermined relations between the Mongols and the Ming dynasty. His policies, particularly the withdrawal of several forward garrisons to the vicinity of the Great Wall, weakened the Ming dynasty's position in the steppe.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988228-159)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
[edit]
Among the Jurchens living in Manchuria, the Ming government sought to maintain peace along the frontier and counter Korean influence. It also aimed to obtain horses and other local products, such as furs, while promoting Chinese culture and values among the Jurchens.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988266%E2%80%93267-161) The Yongle Emperor sent the first mission to Manchuria in 1403, offering Chinese goods and titles in exchange for the Jurchens' recognition of their subordination.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988267-162) From 1411 onwards, the Emperor entrusted the eunuch Yishiha with expeditions to the distant hunting tribes of northern Manchuria.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988267-162) Yishiha's squadron sailed down the Amur River, reaching as far as its mouth at Tyr, and declared the local Jurchens as subjects of the Ming dynasty.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTELevathes1994124%E2%80%93126-163)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
By acknowledging Ming supremacy, the Koreans secured protection against northern tribes, especially the Jurchens, which brought border stability and enhanced the authority of their government through official recognition from China. The ruling Joseon dynasty only came into power in 1392.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-164) The exchange of envoys, which had been frequent under previous emperors, continued during the Yongle Emperor's reign. The Emperor's first ambassadors went to Korea in 1402 to announce his ascension. In the years that followed, there were regular contacts between the two countries, with the Koreans sending two to three delegations per year. The Koreans saw some of the Ming demands as excessive and difficult, but they fulfilled them nonetheless. These demands included providing horses and oxen for military purposes,[[xxix]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-165) bronze Buddha statues, relics, paper for printing Buddhist literature, and even sending girls to serve in the imperial harem.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-164)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
Relations with the Ashikaga government of Japan were at a standstill during the Hongwu era. Hu Weiyong, who was executed in 1380, was accused of conspiring with Japanese assistance.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-166) In 1399, Shōgun Yoshimitsu (r.1369–1408) took the initiative to restore contacts in order to make profit from trade with China.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-167) This led to another mission being sent in 1403, during which the Yongle Emperor's sovereignty was recognized. In 1411, Shōgun Yoshimochi (r.1408–1428) implemented an isolationist policy and interrupted official relations. He also rejected the Ming's attempt to re-establish relations in 1417,[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-166) although strong demand for Chinese goods and coins sustained illegal private trade through the ports of southern Japan.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-167)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-166)

Đại Việt faced growing internal strife by the late 14th century. The kingdom, located in present-day northern Vietnam, was known to the Ming as Annam and ruled by the Trần dynasty. Although the emperor, like his father, was quick to anger and sometimes abused officials cruelly, he built a strong and effective administration, and during his reign China settled into the generally stable political and socioeconomic patterns that were to characterize the remainder of the dynasty.

# Accession to the throne of Yongle
Like his father, Yongle had little personal respect for the higher forms of Chinese culture. In the fashion of the Mongol khans, he summoned to China and highly honoured a Tibetan lama, and the strongest intellectual influence on him may have been that of a monk named Daoyan, a long-favoured personal adviser. Along more orthodox lines, his government sponsored the compilation and publication of Confucian and Neo-Confucian Classics, and it most notably sponsored the preparation in manuscript form of a monumental compendium of literature called _Yongle dadian_ (“The Great Canon of the Yongle Era”) in more than 11,000 volumes, which preserved many works that would otherwise have been lost. But the emperor himself must have considered such activities a kind of busywork for litterateurs who enjoyed public esteem but not his personal trust. A military man of action, the Yongle emperor had little enough patience with unavoidable administrative business, much less with intellectual exercises.

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Mongolian campaigns
The balance of power on the steppe shifted after 1410. In 1412, the Oirat leader Mahmud killed Bunyashiri and established a puppet khan at Karakorum. As he expanded eastward against Arughtai in an apparent attempt to unite the Mongols under his rule, the Oirats emerged as a powerful new force. Their rise alarmed the Ming court and prompted the Yongle Emperor to launch a second campaign into Mongolia in 1414.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988226-154) The Oirat cavalry suffered heavy losses in a battle along the upper Tuul River due to the superior firepower of the Ming artillery. By August, the Emperor was content with the situation and returned to Beijing.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988227-157)
Renewed hostilities erupted in 1421 when the Eastern Mongols launched cross-border raids. The Emperor decided to march against them in 1422, 1423, and 1424 despite opposition from his ministers. His efforts were ultimately unsuccessful. The campaign was costly and achieved few tangible results, largely because the Mongols avoided direct confrontation with the advancing Ming armies.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988227%E2%80%93228-158) The Emperor died while returning from his fifth campaign in Mongolia.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988228-159)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Mongolian campaigns
The Emperor had been unable to subdue the Mongols. His campaigns into Mongolia did not result in any lasting changes and proved to be extremely costly.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988228-159) Although the Chinese had larger armies, more resources, and better weaponry, the nomads' mobility and the vastness of the battlefield negated these advantages.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWang2011113-160) The Yongle Emperor's policy of exploiting divisions among rival Mongol leaders also proved unsuccessful. Rather than securing Ming influence, it alienated the competing factions and undermined relations between the Mongols and the Ming dynasty. His policies, particularly the withdrawal of several forward garrisons to the vicinity of the Great Wall, weakened the Ming dynasty's position in the steppe.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988228-159)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
[edit]
Among the Jurchens living in Manchuria, the Ming government sought to maintain peace along the frontier and counter Korean influence. It also aimed to obtain horses and other local products, such as furs, while promoting Chinese culture and values among the Jurchens.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988266%E2%80%93267-161) The Yongle Emperor sent the first mission to Manchuria in 1403, offering Chinese goods and titles in exchange for the Jurchens' recognition of their subordination.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988267-162) From 1411 onwards, the Emperor entrusted the eunuch Yishiha with expeditions to the distant hunting tribes of northern Manchuria.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988267-162) Yishiha's squadron sailed down the Amur River, reaching as far as its mouth at Tyr, and declared the local Jurchens as subjects of the Ming dynasty.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTELevathes1994124%E2%80%93126-163)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
By acknowledging Ming supremacy, the Koreans secured protection against northern tribes, especially the Jurchens, which brought border stability and enhanced the authority of their government through official recognition from China. The ruling Joseon dynasty only came into power in 1392.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-164) The exchange of envoys, which had been frequent under previous emperors, continued during the Yongle Emperor's reign. The Emperor's first ambassadors went to Korea in 1402 to announce his ascension. In the years that followed, there were regular contacts between the two countries, with the Koreans sending two to three delegations per year. The Koreans saw some of the Ming demands as excessive and difficult, but they fulfilled them nonetheless. These demands included providing horses and oxen for military purposes,[[xxix]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-165) bronze Buddha statues, relics, paper for printing Buddhist literature, and even sending girls to serve in the imperial harem.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-164)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
Relations with the Ashikaga government of Japan were at a standstill during the Hongwu era. Hu Weiyong, who was executed in 1380, was accused of conspiring with Japanese assistance.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-166) In 1399, Shōgun Yoshimitsu (r.1369–1408) took the initiative to restore contacts in order to make profit from trade with China.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-167) This led to another mission being sent in 1403, during which the Yongle Emperor's sovereignty was recognized. In the same year, the Ming government opened maritime trade offices in Ningbo, Quanzhou, and Guangzhou, which allowed Japanese merchants with government licenses to trade. In 1411, Shōgun Yoshimochi (r.1408–1428) implemented an isolationist policy and interrupted official relations. He also rejected the Ming's attempt to re-establish relations in 1417,[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-166) although strong demand for Chinese goods and coins sustained illegal private trade through the ports of southern Japan.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-167)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-166)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
Đại Việt faced growing internal strife by the late 14th century. The kingdom, located in present-day northern Vietnam, was known to the Ming as Annam and ruled by the Trần dynasty. Lê Quý Ly overthrew the Trần dynasty in 1400 and renamed the state Đại Ngu. The Yongle Emperor recognized the new Viet government and confirmed Lê Quý Ly's son as the ruler of Đại Ngu in the winter of 1403, but relations between the two countries were strained due to escalating border disputes. Lê Quý Ly prepared for the impending conflict and continued to engage in border skirmishes. In the spring of 1406, his soldiers ambushed Ming diplomatic envoys accompanying the Trần pretender.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTETsai2002179-168) The incident prompted the Yongle Emperor to order an invasion. The Ming army had attacked Đại Ngu from two directions by late 1406, and resistance was quelled by mid-1407. In July, the country was officially annexed to the Ming dynasty as Jiaozhi Province.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988230-169)

## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
Supporters of the Trần dynasty launched a rebellion in 1408, but the Ming army defeated them the next year.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988231-170) Another rebellion erupted shortly after and was only fully crushed in 1414 when the Chinese captured the rebel leader, Trần Quý Khoáng. The majority of the Ming army was unable to withdraw until 1416.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988231-170) By the end of 1417, the Viet people launched another rebellion,[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWade200680-171) led by military leader Lê Lợi. The Ming generals were unable to suppress the rebellion until the end of the Yongle Emperor's reign.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTETsai2002184%E2%80%93186-172)[[xxx]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-175)

In 1405, the Yongle Emperor appointed his favorite commander, the eunuch Zheng He, as admiral of a fleet with the purpose of expanding China's influence and collecting tribute from various nations. Title: The Bar Scene in Beijing
Chunks: 0,1
Although most average Chinese still prefer to get drunk at dinner, the Western pub tradition has gained ground among younger locals, and the city has a large, ever-growing population of establishments devoted exclusively to alcohol.
Drinking in Beijing occurs in one of several districts, each with its own atmosphere and social connotations. The city's oldest and still most popular drinking district is **Sanlitun,** located between the East Second and Third ring roads around the Workers' Stadium (Gongren Tiyuchang). The area's name comes from Sanlitun Lu, a north-south strip of drinking establishments a long block east of the Workers' Stadium that at one time contained practically all of the city's bars. Now known as Sanlitun Bar Street (Sanlitun Jiuba Jie), it has been overshadowed by other clusters of bars in the Xingfu Cun area north of the stadium and scattered around the stadium itself. Bars here are rowdy and raunchy, and packed to overflowing on weekends. Similar watering holes surround the south and west gates of **Chaoyang Gongyuan** (park) to the east, an area the government has tried to promote as the new drinking district because it has fewer residential buildings. The development of **Lucky Street,** north of the Kempinski Hotel, followed a similar logic. Bars and clubs in **Haidian,** the city's university district to the northwest, are clustered around the gates of several universities and cater to a crowd of local English majors and foreign students.
The fastest-growing spot for late-night drinking is the **Back Lakes** (**Shicha Hai** or **Hou Hai**), a previously serene spot with a few discreetly fashionable bars north of Bei Hai Park. It has exploded into a riot of neon, capped by Lotus Lane. **Nan Luogu Xiang,** to the east of the Back Lakes area, was previously home to only one cafe; now the bars are wall-to-wall. Perhaps the most notable trend is the resurgence of hotel bars. These are the most appealing and stylish spots in Beijing, most notably **Xiu** and **China Bar** (Park Hyatt), and **Mesh** (The Opposite House).
Beijing bars generally open around 5 or 6pm and stay open until the last patrons leave or the staff decides it wants to go home, usually by 2am on Friday and Saturday nights. Several of the Back Lakes bars double as cafes and open as early as 11am.

**Karaoke: Down That Drink, It's Time to Sing**
No one knows why Asian cultures have embraced karaoke (pronounced "_kala_ okay" in Mandarin) with such red-faced gusto, or why so many foreigners become just as enthusiastic once they're on Eastern soil. Maybe the food lacks some amino acid crucial to the brain's shame function. Or maybe it's just fun to get soused and pretend you have talent, thousands of miles away from home. Spend enough time in Beijing and sooner or later you'll find yourself standing before a TV screen, beer and microphone in hand, with a crowd of drunkards insisting you sing to the Muzak version of a Beatles hit. Refuse and your Chinese host loses face; comply and you receive applause. Resistance is futile. Most karaoke venues in Beijing are seedy and given over to less-than-legal side entertainment, so if you have any choice in the matter, head to **Party World,** also known as the Cash Box (Qian Gui; tel. **010/6588-3333;** 24 hr.), the city's classiest and best-equipped do-it-yourself concert venue. It's located southeast of the Full Link Plaza, at the corner of Chaowai Shichang Jie and Chaowai Nan Jie, and there's another location at Teng Da Da Sha, Xi Zhi Men Wai Dajie (tel. **010/8857-6566** is the reservation service line for both branches). Cash Box has a hotel-like lobby, pleasantly decorated private rooms, and a wide selection of Western songs, with some even released in the past decade. Prices range from ¥60 to ¥360 per hour, depending on the size of the room and night of the week. There's usually a line, so you'll have to give them your name early. You wouldn't want to embarrass yourself anywhere else.

Title: The Bar Scene in Beijing

Although most average Chinese still prefer to get drunk at dinner, the Western pub tradition has gained ground among younger locals, and the city has a large, ever-growing population of establishments devoted exclusively to alcohol.
Drinking in Beijing occurs in one of several districts, each with its own atmosphere and social connotations. The city's oldest and still most popular drinking district is **Sanlitun,** located between the East Second and Third ring roads around the Workers' Stadium (Gongren Tiyuchang). The area's name comes from Sanlitun Lu, a north-south strip of drinking establishments a long block east of the Workers' Stadium that at one time contained practically all of the city's bars. Now known as Sanlitun Bar Street (Sanlitun Jiuba Jie), it has been overshadowed by other clusters of bars in the Xingfu Cun area north of the stadium and scattered around the stadium itself. Bars here are rowdy and raunchy, and packed to overflowing on weekends. Similar watering holes surround the south and west gates of **Chaoyang Gongyuan** (park) to the east, an area the government has tried to promote as the new drinking district because it has fewer residential buildings. The development of **Lucky Street,** north of the Kempinski Hotel, followed a similar logic. Bars and clubs in **Haidian,** the city's university district to the northwest, are clustered around the gates of several universities and cater to a crowd of local English majors and foreign students.
The fastest-growing spot for late-night drinking is the **Back Lakes** (**Shicha Hai** or **Hou Hai**), a previously serene spot with a few discreetly fashionable bars north of Bei Hai Park. It has exploded into a riot of neon, capped by Lotus Lane. **Nan Luogu Xiang,** to the east of the Back Lakes area, was previously home to only one cafe; now the bars are wall-to-wall. Perhaps the most notable trend is the resurgence of hotel bars. These are the most appealing and stylish spots in Beijing, most notably **Xiu** and **China Bar** (Park Hyatt), and **Mesh** (The Opposite House).
Beijing bars generally open around 5 or 6pm and stay open until the last patrons leave or the staff decides it wants to go home, usually by 2am on Friday and Saturday nights. Several of the Back Lakes bars double as cafes and open as early as 11am.

**Karaoke: Down That Drink, It's Time to Sing**
No one knows why Asian cultures have embraced karaoke (pronounced "_kala_ okay" in Mandarin) with such red-faced gusto, or why so many foreigners become just as enthusiastic once they're on Eastern soil. Maybe the food lacks some amino acid crucial to the brain's shame function. Or maybe it's just fun to get soused and pretend you have talent, thousands of miles away from home. Spend enough time in Beijing and sooner or later you'll find yourself standing before a TV screen, beer and microphone in hand, with a crowd of drunkards insisting you sing to the Muzak version of a Beatles hit. Refuse and your Chinese host loses face; comply and you receive applause. Resistance is futile. Most karaoke venues in Beijing are seedy and given over to less-than-legal side entertainment, so if you have any choice in the matter, head to **Party World,** also known as the Cash Box (Qian Gui; tel. **010/6588-3333;** 24 hr.), the city's classiest and best-equipped do-it-yourself concert venue. It's located southeast of the Full Link Plaza, at the corner of Chaowai Shichang Jie and Chaowai Nan Jie, and there's another location at Teng Da Da Sha, Xi Zhi Men Wai Dajie (tel. **010/8857-6566** is the reservation service line for both branches). Cash Box has a hotel-like lobby, pleasantly decorated private rooms, and a wide selection of Western songs, with some even released in the past decade. Prices range from ¥60 to ¥360 per hour, depending on the size of the room and night of the week. There's usually a line, so you'll have to give them your name early. You wouldn't want to embarrass yourself anywhere else.

The Yongle Emperor (reigned 1402 to 1424) was the third, and most famous, ruler of the Ming dynasty. It was he who sent out the huge treasure fleets which sailed into the Indian Ocean and then onward as far as Africa. It was also he who constructed the great palace complex known as the Forbidden City, in Beijing.
Explore History

#### Prince of Yan
He was born with the name Zhu Di, in 1360, the fourth son the Hongwu emperor, the founder of the Ming dynasty. While still a child he was given the title Prince of Yan. At the age of 20 he was sent to live in Beijing and given responsibility for the defence of the north-eastern sector of the Great Wall of China There, he gained experience in military affairs, and proved himself an able soldier and strategist.

#### Rebellion
When the Hongwu emperor died in 1398, the son of Zhu Di’s eldest brother came to the throne as the Jianwen emperor. Soon, the new emperor began to seek to reduce the power of his uncles, and amongst other measures summoned Zhu Di to the capital, Nanjing. Fearing that if he obeyed the summons, he would be executed, Zhu Di rebelled. In the fierce civil war that followed, Zhu Di was victorious, and succeeded in seizing the throne in 1402. He adopted the title Yongle, which means “Perpetual Happiness.”
The Yongle Emperor

#### A new capital
The Yongle Emperor immediately moved the capital from Nanjing (which means “Southern Capital”) to his former base, Beijing (“Northern Capital”). This made strategic sense as it enabled the emperor to have a huge body of troops under his direct command, stationed near the most threatened border of the empire. He personally led several expeditions into the steppes against the Mongols.
Explore History
On the other hand, Beijing was so near the border that it was vulnerable to Mongol attack. The Mongols had, until recently, ruled China and had ambitions to do so again. As Beijing was so far from the more productive parts of the empire (to the south in the Yangtze region), keeping the capital and its large garrison provisioned was hugely expensive. This became a large burden on the Ming state, and involved the refurbishment of the Grand Canal to enable it to carry the vast number of grain transports needed to feed the capital.

#### The Forbidden City
The Yongle Emperor then ordered the construction of the enormous palace complex, set within its own walls and in which the emperor’s family, his harem and his personal staff (the palace eunuchs), were largely secluded from the outside world.
This palace complex became known as the Forbidden City, and was the centre of power of the Ming Dynasty and its successor, the Qing (Manchu) Dynasty. It remains an iconic structure to this day, being a UNESCO heritage site. (Creative Commons Licence)
Explore History

#### The Treasure Fleets
Yongle is most famous for launching seven great naval expeditions “to the Western Ocean” – i.e. the Indian Ocean. He placed one his favourite palace eunuchs, Zheng He, in command of the huge fleets which sailed to Southeast Asia, India, the Persian Gulf, and the East African coast.
These fleets included the treasure ships, which were probably some of the largest sailing vassals ever built. These voyages aimed to display China’s wealth and power, establish tributary relationships with far distant lands, and secure favourable trade relations, expanding China’s influence across Asia and the Indian Ocean.

#### The Yongle Encyclopedia
As well as his more active actions, the Yongle Emperor was also interested in promoting knowledge. He therefore commissioned the _Yongle Encyclopedia_. This was the largest Chinese encyclopedia to be completed in pre-modern times, and attempted to be a compilation of all Chinese knowledge.
Explore History
Yongle died in 1424 while returning from a campaign against the Mongols. His achievements mark him as one of the most consequential of all Chinese emperors.

## Zheng He and the treasure ships
In the sixth month of 1405 the Yongle Emperor sent the eunuch Zheng He to the Western Ocean. The fleet left from Liujiabang in Suzhou, took on final supplies at the Wuhumen anchorage in Fujian, and made Champa its first port. The History of the Ming gives the numbers: 27,800 soldiers and sailors, and sixty-two great ships of 44.4 zhang by 18 zhang, or roughly 140 by 57 meters, to judge by the official figures.
Zheng He was from Kunyang in Yunnan, a Hui Muslim whose family name was Ma. His grandfather and father had both made the pilgrimage to Mecca, which earned them the title hajji. In 1381, when Ming armies took Yunnan, he was captured and castrated, and he ended up in the household of the Prince of Yan. He served in the Jingnan campaign, and the prince gave him the surname Zheng. His background gave him something most civil officials in the capital lacked: a working knowledge of the ports, the monsoon calendar and the languages of the Indian Ocean.
The History of the Ming gives two motives. The Yongle Emperor suspected that the Jianwen emperor had fled overseas and wanted him traced, and he also wanted to display soldiers in foreign lands and show off China’s wealth. One motive was a search, the other a demonstration. There is no reason to choose between them.
The Yongle Emperor’s fleet sailed seven times, from 1405 to 1431, across twenty-eight years. Six voyages belonged to the Yongle reign. The last was sent by the Xuande emperor. It reached more than thirty countries and principalities, and went as far as Mogadishu, Brava and Juba on the East African coast. The route out through the South China Sea, past Malacca and across the Indian Ocean is what is now called the maritime Silk Road.

## Zheng He and the treasure ships
The Yongle Emperor’s fleet did not only carry gifts. On the return in 1405 Zheng He brought back Chen Zuyi, the chief of Palembang, the old capital of Srivijaya. Chen had been raiding merchant shipping. Zheng summoned him, and Chen pretended to surrender while planning an attack. He was defeated, taken, and executed in Nanjing. In 1408 the fleet went to Ceylon, where King Alakeshvara lured Zheng inland, demanded gold, and sent soldiers against his ships. Zheng saw that the army had left and the city was empty, took two thousand men, stormed the capital and captured the king with his wives and officials. He presented the prisoner in 1411. The Yongle Emperor spared him and sent him home. In the winter of 1412 the fleet sailed again and seized Sekandar, a pretender to the throne of Samudra, bringing him back in 1413.
Malacca shows how the Yongle Emperor’s system worked on the ground. The place had been subject to Siam and paid forty ounces of gold a year. In 1409 Zheng He invested the local chief with a silver seal, robes and a stone tablet, and Malacca became a kingdom under Ming protection. When the fleet arrived, it built a stockade with a wall, four gates, drum towers and a night watch, and inside it a second enclosure with warehouses. Ships going to different ports left their goods there and came back to assemble. When the southwest monsoon turned in the middle of the fifth month, the whole fleet left together.
At Calicut a stone inscription survived: "Ten thousand li and more from China, where the people and their goods are at peace and share one custom. Cut in stone here, to be shown forever." Calicut is Kozhikode, on the Malabar coast. Business there had its own form. The broker named a date for the sale, the two sides clapped palms once in front of witnesses, and the price stood.
Once fixed, neither side could reopen it.

## Zheng He and the treasure ships
Under the Yongle Emperor, the system ran on tribute. Foreign courts brought local goods. The Ming gave back silk, porcelain and copper cash, usually more than it received. That practice had a name: give much, receive little. What the court wanted was recognition and order, not annexation, garrisons or governors. Its fleet used force when sea lanes were blocked or a king attacked its ships.
The cost is in the History of the Ming: "The nameless treasures it brought back cannot be counted, and China’s waste was beyond reckoning." In the first month of 1424 Zheng He was still being sent to Palembang with a seal. By the time he returned, the Yongle Emperor was dead. In the second month of 1425 he was posted to command the garrison at Nanjing, the first man to hold that post. In 1431 the Xuande emperor, noting that distant states had stopped coming, sent him out one last time. He died at Calicut in 1433 on the way home. Wang Jinghong brought the fleet back. Zheng He was buried on the southern slope of Ox Head Hill outside Nanjing.
Ninety years later Vasco da Gama reached the same port of Calicut. He had four ships and about 170 men. On his first visit Zheng He had brought sixty-two great ships and 27,800 men.

## The Yongle Encyclopedia
In the seventh month of 1403 the Yongle Emperor ordered Xie Jin, a reader in the Hanlin Academy, to compile a book that would gather material from the classics, histories, philosophical works and belles-lettres by category, so that it could be consulted easily. One hundred and forty-seven scholars worked on it. They delivered in the twelfth month of the following year under the title Wenxian Dacheng, the Great Compendium of Documents.
The Yongle Emperor was not satisfied. It was not complete enough. He added Yao Guangxiao and Liu Jichi to the editorial board and raised the number of editors, copyists and proofreaders to more than three thousand. In the winter of 1408 the work was finished and given the title Yongle Dadian, the Great Canon of the Yongle Reign.
The main text runs to 22,877 juan, with sixty juan of rules and index, bound in 11,095 volumes, about 370 million characters, all copied by hand. Each folio is fifty centimeters tall and thirty wide. The covers are built up from layers of hard-backed paper and wrapped in yellow silk, in the wrapped-back binding used for imperial books. The text is in formal court kaiti. Titles of quoted works are written in red, and the marks for punctuation were stamped with small red circles.
The Yongle Emperor’s compilers arranged the book by the rhyme categories of the Hongwu Zhengyun dictionary. Characters come first, then everything written about them. Under a single character the compilers put its pronunciation, its meanings, its forms in seal, clerical, cursive and regular script, and then extracts from every book that touched on it, sorted by topic. Astronomy goes under heaven. Geography goes under earth. Nothing was rewritten. A sentence, a passage, a chapter, sometimes a whole book, was copied out as it stood.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
Most of the porcelain fired in the Yongle reign was white.
The Chinese name for it, tianbai, means sweet white. The sweetness is about touch. The glaze is opaque and smooth, thick enough to look like set fat. Many pieces are thin enough to be nearly bodiless, so that a hand held behind them shows through. The walls often carry lotus scrolls or flower sprays incised under the glaze, invisible when seen straight on and visible only when the light rakes across them. When archaeologists excavated the imperial kiln site at Zhushan in Jingdezhen, more than ninety-eight percent of the shards in the early Yongle layers were sweet white. This was not an occasional curiosity. It was what the palace used every day.
No source explains why the Yongle Emperor preferred white. A few facts can be set side by side. He had spent nineteen years at Beiping, where the Mongol taste for white still lingered. White porcelain was used in sacrifices and in Buddhist ritual. The tower he began at the Great Bao’en Monastery in 1412 was faced in white porcelain. Three facts point at white. Which one was the cause cannot be said.
The Palace Museum has a sweet white monk’s-cap ewer, with a mouth that rises at the back and dips at the front, shaped like the hat of a Tibetan monk. The form began as a Tibetan water vessel and tea pot and had reached China under the Yuan. The Yongle Emperor’s court made it in white porcelain and sent it back to Tibet.
Bronze images went with the envoys. The gilt bronzes that survive from the Yongle Emperor’s reign often carry six characters incised on the base: bestowed in the Yongle reign of the Great Ming. The word is bestowed, not made. They were gifts, not furnishings. The recipients were Tibetan lords and senior clerics. The bronzes are cast in high-grade copper by the lost-wax method, gilded all over, with faces, robes and lotus seats that combine Tibetan proportion with Chinese modeling.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
The court’s interest in Tibet was diplomatic before it was devotional. In 1403 the Yongle Emperor sent the eunuch Hou Xian with letters and gifts to invite Halima, known in Tibetan sources as Deshin Shekpa, the fifth Karmapa of the Karma Kagyu school. Hou traveled tens of thousands of li and brought him to Nanjing in the twelfth month of 1406. The Yongle Emperor received him in the Hall of Receiving Heaven and loaded him with gifts, with escorts, saddles and utensils largely of gold and silver. In the second month of 1407 a great offering was held at Linggu Monastery for the benefit of Hongwu and Empress Ma, and the court was told of clouds, flowers, sweet dew, blue birds and white elephants. In the third month Halima was titled the Great Treasure Prince of Dharma, with authority over Buddhism in the realm and a seal graded like those of princes.
The Yongle Emperor’s lacquer took another route. After the move to Beijing in 1421, the imperial household workshops set up the Orchard Factory inside the palace city and brought in Zhang Degang, son of the Yuan master Zhang Cheng. He was interviewed, found satisfactory, and given a post in the Directorate of Construction with charge of lacquer production. Carved red lacquer is built up layer by layer, eighty or ninety coats at the low end, more than a hundred at the high end. While the lacquer is still soft the design is drawn on and cut. The Palace Museum’s oval dish with grapes has fruit rising about fifteen millimeters above the surface, close to full sculpture.
The Orchard Factory is not settled history. Su Yuming, Harry Garner and Cai Meifen have all questioned its connection to Yongle lacquer and argued that official carved lacquer in the early fifteenth century was made in workshops in Jiangsu and Zhejiang.
The site is gone.
Much of the Yongle Emperor’s lacquer went to Japan. He sent three missions there, carrying 203 pieces of carved lacquer among the gifts, along with a few incised gold pieces. They entered the Ashikaga storehouses and became part of the shogunate’s collection of Chinese objects. Late Ming connoisseurs judged Yongle lacquer "a cut below the Song, but still fine."

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
In the seventh month of 1424, on the way back from his fifth campaign, the Yongle Emperor fell ill at Yumuchuan. He left an edict naming the crown prince as his successor and ordering a funeral on the Hongwu model. He died on the day recorded as xinmao, at sixty-five.
The Yongle Emperor’s army was still in the steppe. The eunuch Ma Yun, the grand secretary Yang Rong and Jin Youzi decided to keep the death secret, for fear of what the news would do to the troops. They melted tin into an inner coffin, laid the body in it, and set it on the imperial carriage, with meals served morning and evening as usual wherever the column stopped. In the eighth month Yang Rong rode back to Beijing with the news, and the crown prince sent his son to meet the coffin at Kaiping.
The Yongle Emperor was buried at Changling, on the Tianshou range at Changping. The tomb was begun in 1409, the Ling’en Hall was finished in the third month of 1416, and the whole complex was complete in 1427. The Ling’en Hall is the only Ming imperial hall of its kind still standing. It is nine bays wide and five deep, and sixty whole nanmu columns carry the roof. The four in the center bay are the thickest, 1.12 meters across at the base, more than a man can reach around. The Hall of Supreme Harmony in Beijing is more than two centuries later and larger, but its timber is not the original.
The Yongle Emperor’s temple name was Taizong. In the ninth month of 1538 it was changed to Chengzu.
The verdict in the History of the Ming sets two things side by side. The first says his territory "far surpassed that of the Han and Tang" and that some thirty states sent envoys under his command. The second says that "in the matter of the proscription he acted against the grain," and that the shame of it cannot be covered. One sentence covers territory and tribute. The other covers the means by which he took the throne. The editors placed both in the same paragraph and did not let either cancel the other.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
What can be seen of Yongle today is scattered. There is the axis and the stone platform in the Forbidden City, the nanmu hall at Changling, the foundations of the Great Bao’en Monastery in Nanjing, a few hundred volumes in London and Washington, and a room of blue and white in Istanbul.
The Ling’en Hall is still the timber frame finished in 1416, and its sixty nanmu columns were raised then. The timber of the Hall of Supreme Harmony is not.

In the forty-first year of Jiajing (AD 1562), the Jiajing Emperor appointed Gao Gong, Qu Jingchun, Zhang Juzheng, and others to take charge of recopying the Yongle Encyclopedia. The Ministry of Personnel and the Ministry of Rites presided over "sealed-name examinations" and selected 109 skilled calligraphers. The Imperial Household Department allocated painters, polishing craftsmen, paper makers, and others. The Fuel Supply Office, the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and the Hanlin Academy were respectively responsible for supplying charcoal, wine and food, and "monthly rice." The recopying work formally began.
3
It was completed in the early Longqing era, and the original manuscript was returned to Nanjing. Its original copy was stored in the Wenyuan Pavilion, while the duplicate copy was stored separately in Huangshicheng.
5
By the Qianlong era, 8,000 volumes of this work survived, so some suspected that the copying had not been completed at that time. The whereabouts of the original work have remained an unsolved mystery, and historians have offered various conjectures. Gu Yanwu's Record of Daily Knowledge concluded that the encyclopedia was "entirely lost." Another conjecture is that the original was buried with the Jiajing Emperor as a funerary object. After the Jiajing Emperor died, he was not buried immediately but waited a long time; at that time the duplicate copy was being made, and some believe that the burial was delayed until the copying work was completed. In the end, however, the Jiajing duplicate copy contained only 8,000 volumes, leading to suspicion that it may not have been fully copied because of the haste for burial.
7
Qing Dynasty Compilation of Lost Texts

The Yongle Encyclopedia suffered losses as early as the Ming dynasty. Quan Zuwang and Li Fu were both great scholars of the Qing dynasty. During the Yongzheng reign, the Institute for the Three Rites was established; both Quan and Li served at the Hanlin Academy and thus gained access to the Yongle Encyclopedia. In it they saw many books not found elsewhere in the world and exclaimed that they were "prodigious treasures of the universe." After discussing the matter, they decided that they should first compile and extract the books they wished to see but could not obtain. Quan Zuwang wrote the Record of Copying the Yongle Encyclopedia, believing that the five categories most in need of extraction were the classics, histories, local gazetteers, genealogies, and literature. From then on, the two read 20 volumes each day, marked the titles they wished to extract, and had another four people copy them. Working through the material daily in this way, they compiled more than ten works, including Wang Anshi's New Interpretations of the Zhou Officials and Master Gao's Chunqiu Yizong. But how could two people read through the voluminous Yongle Encyclopedia even once? The long-term work of compiling lost texts left both physically and mentally exhausted. The next year, Quan Zuwang was dismissed from office and returned home, so the compilation work had to be abandoned. However, the results of Quan and Li's compilation of lost texts attracted widespread attention among scholars and laid the foundation for the later systematic compilation of lost texts from the Yongle Encyclopedia by the editors of the Siku Quanshu Commission.
9

During the Kangxi and Yongzheng reigns, a large encyclopedic work, the Complete Collection of Illustrations and Writings, was compiled. The Qianlong Emperor strongly disapproved of the format of such encyclopedias. He believed that although encyclopedias could include and record materials from all categories and present a grand view of documents, the method of "selecting according to categories" prevented people from seeing the complete appearance of books, tracing their origins, and verifying their sources. He wanted to do what his predecessors had not done: compile a large series, the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, to remedy the deficiencies of encyclopedias. He also named the pavilions housing the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries with the characters for "deep pool," "source," "ford," and "trace upstream," highlighting that only his work could truly "trace its origins." At this time, Zhu Yun, Anhui Education Commissioner, and Yu Minzhong, Chief Editor of the Siku Quanshu, both suggested to the Qianlong Emperor that the many lost ancient books in the Yongle Encyclopedia be compiled and recovered, which drew the Qianlong Emperor's attention. At the beginning of the establishment of the Siku Quanshu Commission, he issued two imperial edicts in succession, ordering the compilation and collation of rare ancient books in the Yongle Encyclopedia.
Qianlong Emperor (Emperor Gaozong of the Qing)

In the 38th year of the Qianlong reign (1772), the Qing government compiled the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries and discovered that 2,422 volumes, about more than one thousand fascicles, of the Yongle Encyclopedia had been lost or were missing. The editors of the Siku Quanshu Commission recovered a large number of lost books from the Yongle Encyclopedia, of which 385 titles were included in the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries. In the 38th year of the Qianlong reign, the Siku Quanshu Commission collated the Yongle Encyclopedia; 39 people, including the famous scholars Dai Zhen, Shao Jinhan, and Zhou Yongnian of the time, took part in the recovery of lost texts. Among them, Zhou Yongnian worked most diligently on poetry and prose collections of Song and Yuan authors. Shao Jinhan recovered the Old History of the Five Dynasties and Records of the Nine Kingdoms, and Dai Zhen recovered the Mathematical Classics; each also achieved results.
By the 46th year of the Qianlong reign (1781), a total of 385 titles in 4,946 volumes had been recovered in the four divisions of classics, history, masters, and collections. Famous examples include the Old History of the Five Dynasties, later included in the Twenty-Four Histories; the important work Essential Chronicle since the Jianyan Era, which records historical facts of the early Southern Song; the Compendium of Surnames of the Yuanhe Era, used to trace Tang family lineages; the famous bibliographical work Annotated Bibliography of the Zhizhai Studio; and Du Yu of the Western Jin's Explanatory Examples of the Spring and Autumn Annals. As for poetry and prose collections by Song and Yuan authors, they reached 175 titles, and many important lost classics were restored to their original form through this recovery project.

The Qianlong Emperor therefore adhered to Confucian orthodox views in the recovery of lost texts, believing that "the essence has been exhausted and the dregs may be discarded"; he did not recover any Buddhist and Daoist works, drama, fiction, or the like, and showed no mercy toward wording involving offensive or prohibited content, deleting it all. Some works on science and technology, such as Deng Yufu's Agricultural Calendar in 200 volumes, which was more detailed than Essential Techniques for the Welfare of the People, as well as some military inventions, were also discarded and not collected, for fear that foreigners might learn them. Even scattered fragments already recovered, such as Jianjin Hebi and Jinshi Huichen, or important gazetteer-type books that had been marked out, such as the Yuan Unified Gazetteer, were all discarded and ignored.
After the Siku Quanshu Commission carried out a systematic recovery of lost texts from the Yongle Encyclopedia, the historical materials in the Encyclopedia were used during the Jiaqing reign when compiling the Complete Prose of the Tang and the Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Great Qing. However, the greatest contribution was Xu Song's recovery work: his recovered Song Huiyao in 500 volumes, Ritual Books of the Song Restoration, Continued Ritual Books of the Song Restoration, and Gazetteer of Henan under the Yuan were all large works of more than 100 volumes. Later, Wen Tingshi recovered Records of the Yuan Dynasty and Charts of Song Top Graduates, among others; Miao Quansun recovered the Gazetteer of Luzhou under the Ming and the Gazetteer of Shuntian Prefecture in the Yongle Era of the Ming; and Dong Kang recovered the Comprehensive Records of the Censorate.
Modern Loss Abroad
In the 10th year of the Xianfeng reign (1860), the Anglo-French Expedition occupied Beijing; the Hanlin Academy was looted, and a large number of volumes of the Yongle Encyclopedia were lost.

The Yongle Emperor (reigned 1402 to 1424) was the third, and most famous, ruler of the Ming dynasty. It was he who sent out the huge treasure fleets which sailed into the Indian Ocean and then onward as far as Africa. It was also he who constructed the great palace complex known as the Forbidden City, in Beijing.
Explore History
texts.1:
#### Prince of Yan
He was born with the name Zhu Di, in 1360, the fourth son the Hongwu emperor, the founder of the Ming dynasty. While still a child he was given the title Prince of Yan. At the age of 20 he was sent to live in Beijing and given responsibility for the defence of the north-eastern sector of the Great Wall of China There, he gained experience in military affairs, and proved himself an able soldier and strategist.
texts.2:
#### Rebellion
When the Hongwu emperor died in 1398, the son of Zhu Di’s eldest brother came to the throne as the Jianwen emperor. Soon, the new emperor began to seek to reduce the power of his uncles, and amongst other measures summoned Zhu Di to the capital, Nanjing. Fearing that if he obeyed the summons, he would be executed, Zhu Di rebelled. In the fierce civil war that followed, Zhu Di was victorious, and succeeded in seizing the throne in 1402. He adopted the title Yongle, which means “Perpetual Happiness.”
The Yongle Emperor
texts.3:
#### A new capital
The Yongle Emperor immediately moved the capital from Nanjing (which means “Southern Capital”) to his former base, Beijing (“Northern Capital”). This made strategic sense as it enabled the emperor to have a huge body of troops under his direct command, stationed near the most threatened border of the empire. He personally led several expeditions into the steppes against the Mongols.
Explore History
On the other hand, Beijing was so near the border that it was vulnerable to Mongol attack. The Mongols had, until recently, ruled China and had ambitions to do so again. As Beijing was so far from the more productive parts of the empire (to the south in the Yangtze region), keeping the capital and its large garrison provisioned was hugely expensive. This became a large burden on the Ming state, and involved the refurbishment of the Grand Canal to enable it to carry the vast number of grain transports needed to feed the capital.
texts.4:
#### The Forbidden City
The Yongle Emperor then ordered the construction of the enormous palace complex, set within its own walls and in which the emperor’s family, his harem and his personal staff (the palace eunuchs), were largely secluded from the outside world.
This palace complex became known as the Forbidden City, and was the centre of power of the Ming Dynasty and its successor, the Qing (Manchu) Dynasty. It remains an iconic structure to this day, being a UNESCO heritage site. (Creative Commons Licence)
Explore History
texts.5:
#### The Treasure Fleets
Yongle is most famous for launching seven great naval expeditions “to the Western Ocean” – i.e. the Indian Ocean. He placed one his favourite palace eunuchs, Zheng He, in command of the huge fleets which sailed to Southeast Asia, India, the Persian Gulf, and the East African coast.
These fleets included the treasure ships, which were probably some of the largest sailing vassals ever built. These voyages aimed to display China’s wealth and power, establish tributary relationships with far distant lands, and secure favourable trade relations, expanding China’s influence across Asia and the Indian Ocean.
texts.6:
#### The Yongle Encyclopedia
As well as his more active actions, the Yongle Emperor was also interested in promoting knowledge. He therefore commissioned the _Yongle Encyclopedia_. This was the largest Chinese encyclopedia to be completed in pre-modern times, and attempted to be a compilation of all Chinese knowledge.
Explore History
Yongle died in 1424 while returning from a campaign against the Mongols. His achievements mark him as one of the most consequential of all Chinese emperors.

The Yongle Emperor was not satisfied. It was not complete enough. He added Yao Guangxiao and Liu Jichi to the editorial board and raised the number of editors, copyists and proofreaders to more than three thousand. In the winter of 1408 the work was finished and given the title Yongle Dadian, the Great Canon of the Yongle Reign.
The main text runs to 22,877 juan, with sixty juan of rules and index, bound in 11,095 volumes, about 370 million characters, all copied by hand. Each folio is fifty centimeters tall and thirty wide. The covers are built up from layers of hard-backed paper and wrapped in yellow silk, in the wrapped-back binding used for imperial books. The text is in formal court kaiti. Titles of quoted works are written in red, and the marks for punctuation were stamped with small red circles.
The Yongle Emperor’s compilers arranged the book by the rhyme categories of the Hongwu Zhengyun dictionary. Characters come first, then everything written about them. Under a single character the compilers put its pronunciation, its meanings, its forms in seal, clerical, cursive and regular script, and then extracts from every book that touched on it, sorted by topic. Astronomy goes under heaven. Geography goes under earth. Nothing was rewritten. A sentence, a passage, a chapter, sometimes a whole book, was copied out as it stood.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
Most of the porcelain fired in the Yongle reign was white.
The Chinese name for it, tianbai, means sweet white. The sweetness is about touch. The glaze is opaque and smooth, thick enough to look like set fat. Many pieces are thin enough to be nearly bodiless, so that a hand held behind them shows through. The walls often carry lotus scrolls or flower sprays incised under the glaze, invisible when seen straight on and visible only when the light rakes across them. When archaeologists excavated the imperial kiln site at Zhushan in Jingdezhen, more than ninety-eight percent of the shards in the early Yongle layers were sweet white. This was not an occasional curiosity. It was what the palace used every day.
No source explains why the Yongle Emperor preferred white. A few facts can be set side by side. He had spent nineteen years at Beiping, where the Mongol taste for white still lingered. White porcelain was used in sacrifices and in Buddhist ritual. The tower he began at the Great Bao’en Monastery in 1412 was faced in white porcelain. Three facts point at white. Which one was the cause cannot be said.
The Palace Museum has a sweet white monk’s-cap ewer, with a mouth that rises at the back and dips at the front, shaped like the hat of a Tibetan monk. The form began as a Tibetan water vessel and tea pot and had reached China under the Yuan. The Yongle Emperor’s court made it in white porcelain and sent it back to Tibet.
Bronze images went with the envoys. The gilt bronzes that survive from the Yongle Emperor’s reign often carry six characters incised on the base: bestowed in the Yongle reign of the Great Ming. The word is bestowed, not made. They were gifts, not furnishings. The recipients were Tibetan lords and senior clerics. The bronzes are cast in high-grade copper by the lost-wax method, gilded all over, with faces, robes and lotus seats that combine Tibetan proportion with Chinese modeling.
