## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
The court’s interest in Tibet was diplomatic before it was devotional. In 1403 the Yongle Emperor sent the eunuch Hou Xian with letters and gifts to invite Halima, known in Tibetan sources as Deshin Shekpa, the fifth Karmapa of the Karma Kagyu school. Hou traveled tens of thousands of li and brought him to Nanjing in the twelfth month of 1406. The Yongle Emperor received him in the Hall of Receiving Heaven and loaded him with gifts, with escorts, saddles and utensils largely of gold and silver. In the second month of 1407 a great offering was held at Linggu Monastery for the benefit of Hongwu and Empress Ma, and the court was told of clouds, flowers, sweet dew, blue birds and white elephants. In the third month Halima was titled the Great Treasure Prince of Dharma, with authority over Buddhism in the realm and a seal graded like those of princes.
The Yongle Emperor’s lacquer took another route. After the move to Beijing in 1421, the imperial household workshops set up the Orchard Factory inside the palace city and brought in Zhang Degang, son of the Yuan master Zhang Cheng. He was interviewed, found satisfactory, and given a post in the Directorate of Construction with charge of lacquer production. Carved red lacquer is built up layer by layer, eighty or ninety coats at the low end, more than a hundred at the high end. While the lacquer is still soft the design is drawn on and cut. The Palace Museum’s oval dish with grapes has fruit rising about fifteen millimeters above the surface, close to full sculpture.
The Orchard Factory is not settled history. Su Yuming, Harry Garner and Cai Meifen have all questioned its connection to Yongle lacquer and argued that official carved lacquer in the early fifteenth century was made in workshops in Jiangsu and Zhejiang.
The site is gone.
Much of the Yongle Emperor’s lacquer went to Japan. He sent three missions there, carrying 203 pieces of carved lacquer among the gifts, along with a few incised gold pieces. They entered the Ashikaga storehouses and became part of the shogunate’s collection of Chinese objects. Late Ming connoisseurs judged Yongle lacquer "a cut below the Song, but still fine."

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
In the seventh month of 1424, on the way back from his fifth campaign, the Yongle Emperor fell ill at Yumuchuan. He left an edict naming the crown prince as his successor and ordering a funeral on the Hongwu model. He died on the day recorded as xinmao, at sixty-five.
The Yongle Emperor’s army was still in the steppe. The eunuch Ma Yun, the grand secretary Yang Rong and Jin Youzi decided to keep the death secret, for fear of what the news would do to the troops. They melted tin into an inner coffin, laid the body in it, and set it on the imperial carriage, with meals served morning and evening as usual wherever the column stopped. In the eighth month Yang Rong rode back to Beijing with the news, and the crown prince sent his son to meet the coffin at Kaiping.
The Yongle Emperor was buried at Changling, on the Tianshou range at Changping. The tomb was begun in 1409, the Ling’en Hall was finished in the third month of 1416, and the whole complex was complete in 1427. The Ling’en Hall is the only Ming imperial hall of its kind still standing. It is nine bays wide and five deep, and sixty whole nanmu columns carry the roof. The four in the center bay are the thickest, 1.12 meters across at the base, more than a man can reach around. The Hall of Supreme Harmony in Beijing is more than two centuries later and larger, but its timber is not the original.
The Yongle Emperor’s temple name was Taizong. In the ninth month of 1538 it was changed to Chengzu.
The verdict in the History of the Ming sets two things side by side. The first says his territory "far surpassed that of the Han and Tang" and that some thirty states sent envoys under his command. The second says that "in the matter of the proscription he acted against the grain," and that the shame of it cannot be covered. One sentence covers territory and tribute. The other covers the means by which he took the throne. The editors placed both in the same paragraph and did not let either cancel the other.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
What can be seen of Yongle today is scattered. There is the axis and the stone platform in the Forbidden City, the nanmu hall at Changling, the foundations of the Great Bao’en Monastery in Nanjing, a few hundred volumes in London and Washington, and a room of blue and white in Istanbul.
The Ling’en Hall is still the timber frame finished in 1416, and its sixty nanmu columns were raised then. The timber of the Hall of Supreme Harmony is not.

In the forty-first year of Jiajing (AD 1562), the Jiajing Emperor appointed Gao Gong, Qu Jingchun, Zhang Juzheng, and others to take charge of recopying the Yongle Encyclopedia. The Ministry of Personnel and the Ministry of Rites presided over "sealed-name examinations" and selected 109 skilled calligraphers. The Imperial Household Department allocated painters, polishing craftsmen, paper makers, and others. The Fuel Supply Office, the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and the Hanlin Academy were respectively responsible for supplying charcoal, wine and food, and "monthly rice." The recopying work formally began.
3
It was completed in the early Longqing era, and the original manuscript was returned to Nanjing. Its original copy was stored in the Wenyuan Pavilion, while the duplicate copy was stored separately in Huangshicheng.
5
By the Qianlong era, 8,000 volumes of this work survived, so some suspected that the copying had not been completed at that time. The whereabouts of the original work have remained an unsolved mystery, and historians have offered various conjectures. Gu Yanwu's Record of Daily Knowledge concluded that the encyclopedia was "entirely lost." Another conjecture is that the original was buried with the Jiajing Emperor as a funerary object. After the Jiajing Emperor died, he was not buried immediately but waited a long time; at that time the duplicate copy was being made, and some believe that the burial was delayed until the copying work was completed. In the end, however, the Jiajing duplicate copy contained only 8,000 volumes, leading to suspicion that it may not have been fully copied because of the haste for burial.

The Yongle Encyclopedia suffered losses as early as the Ming dynasty. Quan Zuwang and Li Fu were both great scholars of the Qing dynasty. During the Yongzheng reign, the Institute for the Three Rites was established; both Quan and Li served at the Hanlin Academy and thus gained access to the Yongle Encyclopedia. In it they saw many books not found elsewhere in the world and exclaimed that they were "prodigious treasures of the universe." After discussing the matter, they decided that they should first compile and extract the books they wished to see but could not obtain. Quan Zuwang wrote the Record of Copying the Yongle Encyclopedia, believing that the five categories most in need of extraction were the classics, histories, local gazetteers, genealogies, and literature. From then on, the two read 20 volumes each day, marked the titles they wished to extract, and had another four people copy them. Working through the material daily in this way, they compiled more than ten works, including Wang Anshi's New Interpretations of the Zhou Officials and Master Gao's Chunqiu Yizong. But how could two people read through the voluminous Yongle Encyclopedia even once? The long-term work of compiling lost texts left both physically and mentally exhausted. The next year, Quan Zuwang was dismissed from office and returned home, so the compilation work had to be abandoned. However, the results of Quan and Li's compilation of lost texts attracted widespread attention among scholars and laid the foundation for the later systematic compilation of lost texts from the Yongle Encyclopedia by the editors of the Siku Quanshu Commission.
9

During the Kangxi and Yongzheng reigns, a large encyclopedic work, the Complete Collection of Illustrations and Writings, was compiled. The Qianlong Emperor strongly disapproved of the format of such encyclopedias. He believed that although encyclopedias could include and record materials from all categories and present a grand view of documents, the method of "selecting according to categories" prevented people from seeing the complete appearance of books, tracing their origins, and verifying their sources. He wanted to do what his predecessors had not done: compile a large series, the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, to remedy the deficiencies of encyclopedias. He also named the pavilions housing the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries with the characters for "deep pool," "source," "ford," and "trace upstream," highlighting that only his work could truly "trace its origins." At this time, Zhu Yun, Anhui Education Commissioner, and Yu Minzhong, Chief Editor of the Siku Quanshu, both suggested to the Qianlong Emperor that the many lost ancient books in the Yongle Encyclopedia be compiled and recovered, which drew the Qianlong Emperor's attention. At the beginning of the establishment of the Siku Quanshu Commission, he issued two imperial edicts in succession, ordering the compilation and collation of rare ancient books in the Yongle Encyclopedia.
Qianlong Emperor (Emperor Gaozong of the Qing)

In the 38th year of the Qianlong reign (1772), the Qing government compiled the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries and discovered that 2,422 volumes, about more than one thousand fascicles, of the Yongle Encyclopedia had been lost or were missing. The editors of the Siku Quanshu Commission recovered a large number of lost books from the Yongle Encyclopedia, of which 385 titles were included in the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries. In the 38th year of the Qianlong reign, the Siku Quanshu Commission collated the Yongle Encyclopedia; 39 people, including the famous scholars Dai Zhen, Shao Jinhan, and Zhou Yongnian of the time, took part in the recovery of lost texts. Among them, Zhou Yongnian worked most diligently on poetry and prose collections of Song and Yuan authors. Shao Jinhan recovered the Old History of the Five Dynasties and Records of the Nine Kingdoms, and Dai Zhen recovered the Mathematical Classics; each also achieved results.
By the 46th year of the Qianlong reign (1781), a total of 385 titles in 4,946 volumes had been recovered in the four divisions of classics, history, masters, and collections. Famous examples include the Old History of the Five Dynasties, later included in the Twenty-Four Histories; the important work Essential Chronicle since the Jianyan Era, which records historical facts of the early Southern Song; the Compendium of Surnames of the Yuanhe Era, used to trace Tang family lineages; the famous bibliographical work Annotated Bibliography of the Zhizhai Studio; and Du Yu of the Western Jin's Explanatory Examples of the Spring and Autumn Annals. As for poetry and prose collections by Song and Yuan authors, they reached 175 titles, and many important lost classics were restored to their original form through this recovery project.
texts.8:
The Qianlong Emperor therefore adhered to Confucian orthodox views in the recovery of lost texts, believing that "the essence has been exhausted and the dregs may be discarded"; he did not recover any Buddhist and Daoist works, drama, fiction, or the like, and showed no mercy toward wording involving offensive or prohibited content, deleting it all. Some works on science and technology, such as Deng Yufu's Agricultural Calendar in 200 volumes, which was more detailed than Essential Techniques for the Welfare of the People, as well as some military inventions, were also discarded and not collected, for fear that foreigners might learn them. Even scattered fragments already recovered, such as Jianjin Hebi and Jinshi Huichen, or important gazetteer-type books that had been marked out, such as the Yuan Unified Gazetteer, were all discarded and ignored.
After the Siku Quanshu Commission carried out a systematic recovery of lost texts from the Yongle Encyclopedia, the historical materials in the Encyclopedia were used during the Jiaqing reign when compiling the Complete Prose of the Tang and the Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Great Qing. However, the greatest contribution was Xu Song's recovery work: his recovered Song Huiyao in 500 volumes, Ritual Books of the Song Restoration, Continued Ritual Books of the Song Restoration, and Gazetteer of Henan under the Yuan were all large works of more than 100 volumes. Later, Wen Tingshi recovered Records of the Yuan Dynasty and Charts of Song Top Graduates, among others; Miao Quansun recovered the Gazetteer of Luzhou under the Ming and the Gazetteer of Shuntian Prefecture in the Yongle Era of the Ming; and Dong Kang recovered the Comprehensive Records of the Censorate.
Modern Loss Abroad
In the 10th year of the Xianfeng reign (1860), the Anglo-French Expedition occupied Beijing; the Hanlin Academy was looted, and a large number of volumes of the Yongle Encyclopedia were lost.

The Yongle Emperor (reigned 1402 to 1424) was the third, and most famous, ruler of the Ming dynasty. It was he who sent out the huge treasure fleets which sailed into the Indian Ocean and then onward as far as Africa. It was also he who constructed the great palace complex known as the Forbidden City, in Beijing.
Explore History

#### Prince of Yan
He was born with the name Zhu Di, in 1360, the fourth son the Hongwu emperor, the founder of the Ming dynasty. While still a child he was given the title Prince of Yan. At the age of 20 he was sent to live in Beijing and given responsibility for the defence of the north-eastern sector of the Great Wall of China There, he gained experience in military affairs, and proved himself an able soldier and strategist.

#### Rebellion
When the Hongwu emperor died in 1398, the son of Zhu Di’s eldest brother came to the throne as the Jianwen emperor. Soon, the new emperor began to seek to reduce the power of his uncles, and amongst other measures summoned Zhu Di to the capital, Nanjing. Fearing that if he obeyed the summons, he would be executed, Zhu Di rebelled. In the fierce civil war that followed, Zhu Di was victorious, and succeeded in seizing the throne in 1402. He adopted the title Yongle, which means “Perpetual Happiness.”
The Yongle Emperor

#### A new capital
The Yongle Emperor immediately moved the capital from Nanjing (which means “Southern Capital”) to his former base, Beijing (“Northern Capital”). This made strategic sense as it enabled the emperor to have a huge body of troops under his direct command, stationed near the most threatened border of the empire. He personally led several expeditions into the steppes against the Mongols.
Explore History
On the other hand, Beijing was so near the border that it was vulnerable to Mongol attack. The Mongols had, until recently, ruled China and had ambitions to do so again. As Beijing was so far from the more productive parts of the empire (to the south in the Yangtze region), keeping the capital and its large garrison provisioned was hugely expensive. This became a large burden on the Ming state, and involved the refurbishment of the Grand Canal to enable it to carry the vast number of grain transports needed to feed the capital.

#### The Forbidden City
The Yongle Emperor then ordered the construction of the enormous palace complex, set within its own walls and in which the emperor’s family, his harem and his personal staff (the palace eunuchs), were largely secluded from the outside world.
This palace complex became known as the Forbidden City, and was the centre of power of the Ming Dynasty and its successor, the Qing (Manchu) Dynasty. It remains an iconic structure to this day, being a UNESCO heritage site. (Creative Commons Licence)
Explore History

#### The Treasure Fleets
Yongle is most famous for launching seven great naval expeditions “to the Western Ocean” – i.e. the Indian Ocean. He placed one his favourite palace eunuchs, Zheng He, in command of the huge fleets which sailed to Southeast Asia, India, the Persian Gulf, and the East African coast.
These fleets included the treasure ships, which were probably some of the largest sailing vassals ever built. These voyages aimed to display China’s wealth and power, establish tributary relationships with far distant lands, and secure favourable trade relations, expanding China’s influence across Asia and the Indian Ocean.

#### The Yongle Encyclopedia
As well as his more active actions, the Yongle Emperor was also interested in promoting knowledge. He therefore commissioned the _Yongle Encyclopedia_. This was the largest Chinese encyclopedia to be completed in pre-modern times, and attempted to be a compilation of all Chinese knowledge.
Explore History
Yongle died in 1424 while returning from a campaign against the Mongols. His achievements mark him as one of the most consequential of all Chinese emperors.

## Zheng He and the treasure ships
In the sixth month of 1405 the Yongle Emperor sent the eunuch Zheng He to the Western Ocean. The History of the Ming gives the numbers: 27,800 soldiers and sailors, and sixty-two great ships of 44.4 zhang by 18 zhang, or roughly 140 by 57 meters, to judge by the official figures.
Zheng He was from Kunyang in Yunnan, a Hui Muslim whose family name was Ma. His grandfather and father had both made the pilgrimage to Mecca, which earned them the title hajji. In 1381, when Ming armies took Yunnan, he was captured and castrated, and he ended up in the household of the Prince of Yan. He served in the Jingnan campaign, and the prince gave him the surname Zheng. His background gave him something most civil officials in the capital lacked: a working knowledge of the ports, the monsoon calendar and the languages of the Indian Ocean.
The History of the Ming gives two motives. The Yongle Emperor suspected that the Jianwen emperor had fled overseas and wanted him traced, and he also wanted to display soldiers in foreign lands and show off China’s wealth. One motive was a search, the other a demonstration. There is no reason to choose between them.
The Yongle Emperor’s fleet sailed seven times, from 1405 to 1431, across twenty-eight years. Six voyages belonged to the Yongle reign. The last was sent by the Xuande emperor. It reached more than thirty countries and principalities, and went as far as Mogadishu, Brava and Juba on the East African coast. The Yongle Emperor’s compilers arranged the book by the rhyme categories of the Hongwu Zhengyun dictionary. Characters come first, then everything written about them. Under a single character the compilers put its pronunciation, its meanings, its forms in seal, clerical, cursive and regular script, and then extracts from every book that touched on it, sorted by topic. Astronomy goes under heaven. Geography goes under earth. Nothing was rewritten. A sentence, a passage, a chapter, sometimes a whole book, was copied out as it stood.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
Most of the porcelain fired in the Yongle reign was white.
The Chinese name for it, tianbai, means sweet white. The sweetness is about touch. The glaze is opaque and smooth, thick enough to look like set fat. Many pieces are thin enough to be nearly bodiless, so that a hand held behind them shows through. The walls often carry lotus scrolls or flower sprays incised under the glaze, invisible when seen straight on and visible only when the light rakes across them. When archaeologists excavated the imperial kiln site at Zhushan in Jingdezhen, more than ninety-eight percent of the shards in the early Yongle layers were sweet white. This was not an occasional curiosity. It was what the palace used every day.
No source explains why the Yongle Emperor preferred white. A few facts can be set side by side. He had spent nineteen years at Beiping, where the Mongol taste for white still lingered. White porcelain was used in sacrifices and in Buddhist ritual. The tower he began at the Great Bao’en Monastery in 1412 was faced in white porcelain. Three facts point at white. Which one was the cause cannot be said.
The Palace Museum has a sweet white monk’s-cap ewer, with a mouth that rises at the back and dips at the front, shaped like the hat of a Tibetan monk. The form began as a Tibetan water vessel and tea pot and had reached China under the Yuan. The Yongle Emperor’s court made it in white porcelain and sent it back to Tibet.
Bronze images went with the envoys. The gilt bronzes that survive from the Yongle Emperor’s reign often carry six characters incised on the base: bestowed in the Yongle reign of the Great Ming. The word is bestowed, not made. They were gifts, not furnishings. The recipients were Tibetan lords and senior clerics. The bronzes are cast in high-grade copper by the lost-wax method, gilded all over, with faces, robes and lotus seats that combine Tibetan proportion with Chinese modeling.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
The court’s interest in Tibet was diplomatic before it was devotional. In 1403 the Yongle Emperor sent the eunuch Hou Xian with letters and gifts to invite Halima, known in Tibetan sources as Deshin Shekpa, the fifth Karmapa of the Karma Kagyu school. Hou traveled tens of thousands of li and brought him to Nanjing in the twelfth month of 1406. The Yongle Emperor received him in the Hall of Receiving Heaven and loaded him with gifts, with escorts, saddles and utensils largely of gold and silver. In the second month of 1407 a great offering was held at Linggu Monastery for the benefit of Hongwu and Empress Ma, and the court was told of clouds, flowers, sweet dew, blue birds and white elephants. In the third month Halima was titled the Great Treasure Prince of Dharma, with authority over Buddhism in the realm and a seal graded like those of princes.
The Yongle Emperor’s lacquer took another route. After the move to Beijing in 1421, the imperial household workshops set up the Orchard Factory inside the palace city and brought in Zhang Degang, son of the Yuan master Zhang Cheng. He was interviewed, found satisfactory, and given a post in the Directorate of Construction with charge of lacquer production. Carved red lacquer is built up layer by layer, eighty or ninety coats at the low end, more than a hundred at the high end. While the lacquer is still soft the design is drawn on and cut. The Palace Museum’s oval dish with grapes has fruit rising about fifteen millimeters above the surface, close to full sculpture.
The Orchard Factory is not settled history. Su Yuming, Harry Garner and Cai Meifen have all questioned its connection to Yongle lacquer and argued that official carved lacquer in the early fifteenth century was made in workshops in Jiangsu and Zhejiang.
The site is gone.
Much of the Yongle Emperor’s lacquer went to Japan. He sent three missions there, carrying 203 pieces of carved lacquer among the gifts, along with a few incised gold pieces. They entered the Ashikaga storehouses and became part of the shogunate’s collection of Chinese objects. Late Ming connoisseurs judged Yongle lacquer "a cut below the Song, but still fine."

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
In the seventh month of 1424, on the way back from his fifth campaign, the Yongle Emperor fell ill at Yumuchuan. He left an edict naming the crown prince as his successor and ordering a funeral on the Hongwu model. He died on the day recorded as xinmao, at sixty-five.
The Yongle Emperor’s army was still in the steppe. The eunuch Ma Yun, the grand secretary Yang Rong and Jin Youzi decided to keep the death secret, for fear of what the news would do to the troops. They melted tin into an inner coffin, laid the body in it, and set it on the imperial carriage, with meals served morning and evening as usual wherever the column stopped. In the eighth month Yang Rong rode back to Beijing with the news, and the crown prince sent his son to meet the coffin at Kaiping.
The Yongle Emperor was buried at Changling, on the Tianshou range at Changping. The tomb was begun in 1409, the Ling’en Hall was finished in the third month of 1416, and the whole complex was complete in 1427. The Ling’en Hall is the only Ming imperial hall of its kind still standing. It is nine bays wide and five deep, and sixty whole nanmu columns carry the roof. The four in the center bay are the thickest, 1.12 meters across at the base, more than a man can reach around. The Hall of Supreme Harmony in Beijing is more than two centuries later and larger, but its timber is not the original.
The Yongle Emperor’s temple name was Taizong. In the ninth month of 1538 it was changed to Chengzu.
The verdict in the History of the Ming sets two things side by side. The first says his territory "far surpassed that of the Han and Tang" and that some thirty states sent envoys under his command. The second says that "in the matter of the proscription he acted against the grain," and that the shame of it cannot be covered. One sentence covers territory and tribute. The other covers the means by which he took the throne. The editors placed both in the same paragraph and did not let either cancel the other.

## Sweet white porcelain, gilt bronzes and carved lacquer
What can be seen of Yongle today is scattered. There is the axis and the stone platform in the Forbidden City, the nanmu hall at Changling, the foundations of the Great Bao’en Monastery in Nanjing, a few hundred volumes in London and Washington, and a room of blue and white in Istanbul.
The Ling’en Hall is still the timber frame finished in 1416, and its sixty nanmu columns were raised then. The timber of the Hall of Supreme Harmony is not.

The Yongle Encyclopedia suffered losses as early as the Ming dynasty. Quan Zuwang and Li Fu were both great scholars of the Qing dynasty. In it they saw many books not found elsewhere in the world and exclaimed that they were "prodigious treasures of the universe." After discussing the matter, they decided that they should first compile and extract the books they wished to see but could not obtain. Quan Zuwang wrote the Record of Copying the Yongle Encyclopedia, believing that the five categories most in need of extraction were the classics, histories, local gazetteers, genealogies, and literature. From then on, the two read 20 volumes each day, marked the titles they wished to extract, and had another four people copy them. Working through the material daily in this way, they compiled more than ten works, including Wang Anshi's New Interpretations of the Zhou Officials and Master Gao's Chunqiu Yizong. But how could two people read through the voluminous Yongle Encyclopedia even once? The long-term work of compiling lost texts left both physically and mentally exhausted. The next year, Quan Zuwang was dismissed from office and returned home, so the compilation work had to be abandoned. Shao Jinhan recovered the Old History of the Five Dynasties and Records of the Nine Kingdoms, and Dai Zhen recovered the Mathematical Classics; each also achieved results.
By the 46th year of the Qianlong reign (1781), a total of 385 titles in 4,946 volumes had been recovered in the four divisions of classics, history, masters, and collections. The Qianlong Emperor therefore adhered to Confucian orthodox views in the recovery of lost texts, believing that "the essence has been exhausted and the dregs may be discarded"; he did not recover any Buddhist and Daoist works, drama, fiction, or the like, and showed no mercy toward wording involving offensive or prohibited content, deleting it all. In the early years of his reign, he seems to have been fascinated by the regions beyond China’s southern borders, perhaps in part because of rumours that the Jianwen emperor had escaped overseas. In 1403 the Yongle emperor sent out three fleets under eunuch commanders to proclaim his accession throughout Southeast Asia as far as Java and southern India. More vigorously than any other ruler in Chinese history, he sought recognition from faraway potentates in these regions. Throughout his reign “tributary” missions regularly traveled to China from overseas, including local kings of Malacca and Brunei. Most renowned of the Yongle emperor’s many ocean admirals was the Muslim eunuch Zheng He, who led grand armadas on seven great voyages between 1405 and 1433. Zheng He visited no fewer than 37 countries, some as far away as the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, and the east coast of Africa almost as far south as Zanzibar, and from all the states that he visited Zheng He brought home envoys bearing tribute to acknowledge the Yongle emperor’s overlordship.

# Yongle
The emperor similarly sent a eunuch emissary on repeated tribute-seeking missions to Tibet and Nepal and a civil servant across Central Asia to Afghanistan and Russian Turkistan. The Yongle emperor became the only ruler in Chinese history to be acknowledged suzerain by the Japanese, under the Ashikaga shogun Yoshimitsu. For a short time the Japanese were so docile as to send their own subjects to the Chinese court for punishment as piratical plunderers of the Korean and Chinese coasts. But the succession of a new shogun brought about a less submissive attitude in Japan; from 1411 on, no tribute missions arrived from Japan despite the Yongle emperor’s inquiries, and Japanese raiders became active again on China’s coast. The emperor then threatened to send a punitive expedition against Japan if it would not reform. But in 1419, when the shogunate brusquely denied responsibility for any piratical activities and refused to resume the former tributary relationship, the Yongle emperor was too preoccupied with other matters to do more than grumble.
The Yongle emperor’s expansionist inclinations led China into an ultimately disastrous military adventure against China’s southern neighbour, Dai Viet (Vietnam, called Annam by the Chinese). In 1400 the young Tran dynasty, heir to the Dai Viet throne, had been deposed and a new dynasty proclaimed. From the beginning of Yongle’s reign Tran loyalist refugees urged him to intervene and restore legitimate rule, and, when his own envoys to Annam were murdered, in 1406, the emperor authorized a punitive campaign. Chinese forces rapidly occupied and pacified Annam. Because no Tran heir seemed available, the Yongle emperor in 1407 transformed Dai Viet from a tributary state into the new Chinese province of Annam. Local resistance broke out almost immediately and continued irrepressibly. Especially after 1418, guerrilla warfare against the Ming authorities made the Chinese position in Annam increasingly precarious. By that time the emperor had lost most of his early interest in the southern regions, and the situation was allowed to deteriorate until his grandson, the Xuande emperor, realistically, albeit with some humiliation, abandoned direct Ming rule of Annam in 1428.

# Yongle
During the early years of the Yongle emperor’s reign, the northern frontier, traditionally the zone of greatest danger to any Chinese regime, was relatively quiescent. At the outset of his Beijing-based insurrection in 1402, the Yongle emperor had sought and won the support of the Mongol tribes directly to his rear, in northeastern China. In later payment for this support, he in effect gave these Urianghad Mongols virtual autonomy by withdrawing China’s command posts south of the Great Wall, and he regularly sent the Urianghad chiefs substantial gifts. Other tribes beyond the northern frontier—the Eastern Mongols, or Tatars, and the Western Mongols, or Oyrats—were too disorganized to do more than struggle among themselves. In the far west, the Turko-Mongol empire builder Timur (Tamerlane) had already invaded and pillaged both India and Syria when the Yongle emperor came to the Chinese throne, and in 1404 Timur prepared to launch an expedition against China. Vaguely aware of this, the Yongle emperor alerted his commanders in the west to prepare for trouble; but Timur died in 1405, and the expedition was canceled. Thereafter, the emperor maintained amicable relations with Timur’s heirs at Samarkand and Herat, keeping the Central Asian trade routes open.

# Yongle
After his early years on the throne, the Yongle emperor’s attention was diverted from the south back to the northern frontier by the emergence of an effective new Tatar leader named Aruqtai. In 1410 the Yongle emperor resumed the aggressive extramural patrolling in the north that had preoccupied him as a prince in the 1380s and ’90s. Between 1410 and 1424 the emperor five times personally led grand armies northward into the Gobi, primarily against Aruqtai but occasionally against Oyrats or restless Urianghad groups. The campaigns culminated in only a few battles, in which the Chinese forces won indecisive victories, but they had the effect of forestalling the development of a new large-scale Mongol confederation that might have seriously threatened China. Astute diplomacy was also relied on during these years to keep the Mongols fragmented and to establish at least nominal Chinese authority over the Juchen (Chinese: Nüzchen, or Ruzhen) peoples in the far northeast, as distant as the Amur River (Chinese: Heilong Jiang).

## Transfer of the capital to Beijing
The most notable domestic event of the Yongle emperor’s reign was the transfer of the national capital and the central government from Nanjing to Beijing. This reflected and symbolized the emperor’s and the country’s shift of attention from the southern oceans to the northern land frontiers. Beijing was perhaps not the ideal site for the national capital: it historically had been associated primarily with “barbarian” dynasties such as the Yuan, it was far removed from China’s economic and cultural heartland, and it was dangerously close and exposed to the northern frontier. But it was the Yongle emperor’s personal power base, and it was a site from which the northern defenses could be kept under effective surveillance. In 1407 the emperor authorized transfer of the capital there, and from 1409 on he spent most of his time in the north. In 1417 large-scale work began on the reconstruction of Beijing, and thereafter the Yongle emperor never returned to Nanjing. The new Beijing palace was completed in 1420, and on New Year’s Day of 1421 Beijing formally became the national capital.

The Hongwu Emperor's rule significantly shaped later Chinese history through his efforts to consolidate power and revive Chinese traditions. To counter Mongol influences, Hongwu modeled his court on the Mongol court, paradoxically reinforcing the centralization of power. He also implemented a military system where soldiers were granted land for cultivation, easing the burden on the populace.
Moreover, Hongwu's emphasis on education and the civil service examination system ensured the recruitment of talented individuals into government, though it also fostered a rigid adherence to Neo-Confucian interpretations. His complex relationship with the scholar class, marked by both encouragement and suppression, reflected his view of scholars as servants of the state.

## Early life
The future Hongwu emperor was born in 1328 as Zhu Chongba, a poor peasant of Haozhou (about 100 miles [160 km] northwest of Nanjing, near China’s east coast). Orphaned at 16, he became a monk at the Huangjue monastery near Fengyang to avoid starvation—a common practice for the sons of poor peasants. As a wandering mendicant, he often begged for food at Hefei (some 100 miles west of Nanjing) and surrounding areas, where no constituted authority existed. Indeed, all of central and northern China was suffering from drought and famine, and more than seven million people starved, a situation that encouraged the popular rebellions that started from around 1325. Led by plebeian bandits, the rebels attacked the rich, distributing their wealth and goods among the people.

**The Fate of the Archives and Historical Source Issues**
According to the "Shuyu Zhouzilu" (written by Yan Congjian, completed in 1574), when the Chenghua Emperor (Xianzong) sought records of the Zheng He expeditions during the Chenghua era (1465–1487), the Ministry of War official Liu Daxia (1436–1516) is said to have stated: "The voyages of Sanbao to the Western Ocean wasted tens of thousands of money and grain, and the deaths of soldiers and civilians numbered in the tens of thousands. Even if rare treasures were brought back, what benefit is there to the state? This is truly a harmful policy, and one that ministers should earnestly remonstrate against."
It is also said that Liu Daxia hid or destroyed the archives, but this anecdote itself is a record from about 100 years after the event, and its accuracy as a historical fact is debated. Furthermore, recent research (Li Yingfa, 2014) has proposed the theory that what Liu Daxia hid or destroyed were the records of the Annam expedition, not the records of the Zheng He voyages.
In any case, since the "Zheng He Navigation Chart" contained in the "Wubeizhi" (compiled by Mao Yuanyi, 1621, published 1628) still exists, not all records were lost. This navigation chart records the route from Nanjing to the coast of East Africa and is considered academically important as the only surviving navigational record of the Zheng He expeditions.
**Maritime Expeditions from the Perspective of International Relations Theory**
**Hegemonic Stability Theory** provides one analytical framework. This theory allows for a view that sees Ming China as a regional hegemon that projected naval superiority to create a "Pax Sinica" (Chinese peace) or "pax Ming" (Ming peace) similar to the later "Pax Britannica" or "Pax Americana." According to this interpretation, the hegemonic order provided stability to the trade networks along the Indian Ocean coast.

However, there are dissenting views on this interpretation. Recent research has questioned whether the Ming dynasty functioned as the "stability provider" assumed by hegemonic stability theory. There is also a view that the Ming economy did not depend on maritime trade (most tax revenue came from agriculture) and that the expeditions were conducted to demonstrate power and status rather than to support the interests of Chinese merchants. The "pax Ming" discussed by Geoff Wade (2005) is also depicted as an "aggressive attempt at maritime dominance" rather than peaceful stability.
**Soft Power Projection** provides an alternative lens. An analysis by James R. Holmes and Toshi Yoshihara (2006) published in the U.S. Naval Institute's Proceedings describes the expeditions as "soft power at sea." The gifting of silk textiles, porcelain, and diplomatic recognition functioned through attraction rather than coercion. The tribute system provided participants with benefits such as protection, trading rights, and recognition of legitimacy. Holmes and Yoshihara argue that modern China is using Zheng He to build a "maritime diplomacy that confers legitimacy on China's naval ambitions and eases the concerns of coastal nations."
**The Cosmological View of Tianxia** provides an indigenous theoretical foundation. "Tianxia" (all under heaven) is a world order concept rooted in classical Chinese thought, based on the ideal of a "world without an outside" (wuwai). According to Zhao Tingyang (2021), this system rejects the binary opposition of friend and enemy and aims for an inclusive order that acknowledges differences without aiming for the annihilation of the other.
David Kang (2010) characterizes the tribute system as a combination of "hierarchy in form and flexibility in practice." China was positioned at the apex as the source of Confucian civilization, but in actual relationships, reciprocity and flexibility were observed. According to Kang, evidence that secondary states viewed this hierarchical order as legitimate can be found in the voluntary adoption of Confucian institutions and the mutual use of the tribute system.
Feng Zhang (2015) demonstrates that tribute diplomacy combined both "instrumental rationality" (maximization of self-interest) and "expressive rationality" (behavior based on Confucian sentiment and duty). Expressive rationality is a feature that has been little conceptualized in Western-centric international relations theory and was an essential component in the regional relations of the Ming dynasty.

**Academic Debate**
The academic debate over the nature of the Zheng He expeditions is not a simple binary opposition but can be classified into three main positions.
**The "Voyages of Friendship" interpretation** is mainly found in the official views of the Chinese government and academic literature within China. Premier Wen Jiabao (2004) stated that they "brought silk, tea, and Chinese culture, but did not occupy an inch of land," and Ambassador Guo Chongli characterized them as "voyages for friendship, not for resource plunder." This interpretation emphasizes the absence of permanent colonial bases and the lack of systematic exploitation.
**Proto-colonialist interpretations** are argued by Geoff Wade (Asia Research Institute, National University of Singapore, 2004/2005) and Charles Horner (Hudson Institute, 2009). Wade defines the expeditions as "maritime proto-colonialism," specifying it as "an early form of maritime colonialism in which a dominant maritime power, through force or the threat thereof, controlled key port cities in major East-West maritime trade networks." In "Rising China and Its Postmodern Fate," Horner argues that the Zheng He fleet engaged in "gunboat diplomacy" and was "exactly like other imperialist powers."
The grounds supporting this interpretation include the following:

*   **Military composition**: According to the "Veritable Records of the Ming" (Taizong Shilu), in a 1405 imperial decree, Zheng He was ordered to "lead 27,000 troops to the Western Ocean." Wade estimates that out of the 28,000 expedition personnel, approximately 26,000 were military personnel.

*   **Palembang attack (1407)**: Defeated the fleet of pirate Chen Zuyi, killing 5,000 people, and appointed Shi Jinqing as the "Pacification Commissioner of Old Port" (Jiugang Xuanweishi), establishing a Ming vassal state.

*   **Ceylon military intervention (1410-1411)**: Captured King Alakeshvara and escorted him to Nanjing, installing the pro-Ming Parakramabahu VI.

*   **Sumatra intervention (1415)**: Subdued and captured the usurper Sekandar, executing him in Nanjing.

*   **Malacca as a strategic base**: Constructed warehouses, granaries, and stockades, and in 1411, escorted King Parameswara and his 540-person entourage to China.
**Intermediate and power-projection interpretations** also exist. Edward Dreyer (2007) concluded that "a thorough examination of primary sources reveals that the purpose of the voyages was not mere exploration but in fact 'power projection'," clearly rejecting the "voyages of friendship" theory. Louise Levathes (1994), while describing it as an "age of exploration and conquest," presents a more complex picture, arguing that China "could have colonized but chose not to."
Note that caution is required with the term "vassal states." What the Ming dynasty established was a **tributary relationship**, where foreign monarchs acknowledged the superiority of the Emperor, performed the kowtow, and received investiture, but there was no permanent military garrisoning in the Western colonial sense. Tansen Sen proposes the term "Mingism" rather than "imperialism."

## Foreign policy
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
By acknowledging their subordination to the Ming emperors, the Koreans were able to secure their northern border. This not only brought stability to the border, but also strengthened the legitimacy of the Korean government through official recognition from China. The ruling Joseon dynasty only came into power in 1392.[[169]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-193) The exchange of envoys, which had been frequent under previous emperors, continued during the Yongle Emperor's reign. The Yongle Emperor's first ambassadors arrived in Korea in 1402 to announce the new emperor's ascension. In the years that followed, there were regular contacts between the two countries, with the Koreans sending two to three delegations per year. Some of the Ming's demands were seen as excessive and difficult by the Koreans, but they still fulfilled them. These demands included providing horses and oxen for military purposes,[[xxv]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-194) bronze Buddha statues, relics, paper for printing Buddhist literature, and even sending girls to serve in the imperial harem.[[169]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-193) However, the Koreans maintained their autonomy in internal affairs.

## Foreign policy
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
During the Hongwu era, relations with the Ashikaga government of Japan were at a standstill. Hu Weiyong, who was executed in 1380, was accused of conspiring with Japanese assistance.[[170]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-195) However, in 1399, Shōgun Yoshimitsu took the initiative to restore contacts in order to make profit from trade with China.[[171]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-196) This led to another mission being sent in 1403, during which the Yongle Emperor's sovereignty was recognized. In the same year, the Ming government opened maritime trade offices in Ningbo, Quanzhou, and Guangzhou, which allowed Japanese merchants with government licenses to trade. However, in 1411, new Shōgun Yoshimochi implemented an isolationist policy and interrupted official relations. He also rejected the Ming's attempt to re-establish relations in 1417.[[170]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-195) Despite this, the allure of Chinese coins and goods was too strong for the Japanese to resist,[[171]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-196) and illegal private trade continued from the ports of southern Japan.[[170]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-195)

## Foreign policy
### Đại Việt
In the late 14th century, Đại Việt (present-day northern Vietnam) was facing internal weakness. In 1400, Lê Quý Ly overthrew the Trần dynasty and changed the name of the state to Đại Ngu. Despite pleas from Viet refugees to the Ming government to restore the fallen dynasty, the Yongle Emperor recognized the new Viet government and confirmed Lê Quý Ly's son as the ruler of Đại Ngu in the winter of 1403. However, relations between the two countries were strained due to escalating border disputes. Lê Quý Ly prepared for the impending conflict and continued to engage in border skirmishes. In the spring of 1406, his soldiers even ambushed a Ming diplomatic envoys accompanying the Trần pretender.[[172]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTETsai2002179-197) In response, the Yongle Emperor ordered an invasion. By late 1406, the Ming army had attacked Đại Ngu from two directions, quelling resistance by mid-1407. In July, the country was officially annexed to the Ming dynasty as Jiaozhi Province.[[173]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988230-198)

## Foreign policy
### Đại Việt
In 1408, a rebellion led by supporters of the Trần dynasty broke out and was eventually suppressed by the Ming army in 1409.[[174]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988231-199) However, this was not the end of unrest as another rebellion erupted shortly after and was only fully crushed in 1414 when the Chinese captured the rebel leader, Trần Quý Khoáng. Despite this, the majority of the Ming army was unable to withdraw until 1416.[[174]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988231-199) By the end of 1417, the Viet people rose up in rebellion once again.[[175]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWade200686-200) This time, they were led by Lê Lợi, a skilled military leader who gained widespread support from the population. Despite their efforts, until the end of the Yongle Emperor's reign, the Ming generals were unable to suppress the rebellion.[[xxvi]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-203)

## Foreign policy
### Other Southeast Asian countries
A memorial stele erected in Nanjing in honor of the Sultan of Brunei, who died here in 1408.
In Southeast Asia, the Ming dynasty had a strong presence during the Yongle era. From 1402 to 1424, the Ming government sent 62 missions to Southeast Asian countries and states (excluding Đại Việt), and received 95 in return.[[178]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988270-204) This included important countries such as Champa, Malacca, Ayutthaya (in present-day Thailand), Majapahit (centered in Java), Samudera in Sumatra, Khmer, and Brunei, all of which paid tribute to the Yongle Emperor. These local rulers sent precious metals, spices, and rare animals to China, and in return received Chinese goods and coins.[[179]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988271-205) The Ming government showed a strong interest in trade and left a lasting impression of their naval power in Southeast Asia, although their focus shifted to northern affairs after 1413.[[180]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988272-206)

# Yongle
The emperor similarly sent a eunuch emissary on repeated tribute-seeking missions to Tibet and Nepal and a civil servant across Central Asia to Afghanistan and Russian Turkistan. The Yongle emperor became the only ruler in Chinese history to be acknowledged suzerain by the Japanese, under the Ashikaga shogun Yoshimitsu. For a short time the Japanese were so docile as to send their own subjects to the Chinese court for punishment as piratical plunderers of the Korean and Chinese coasts. But the succession of a new shogun brought about a less submissive attitude in Japan; from 1411 on, no tribute missions arrived from Japan despite the Yongle emperor’s inquiries, and Japanese raiders became active again on China’s coast. The emperor then threatened to send a punitive expedition against Japan if it would not reform. But in 1419, when the shogunate brusquely denied responsibility for any piratical activities and refused to resume the former tributary relationship, the Yongle emperor was too preoccupied with other matters to do more than grumble.
The Yongle emperor’s expansionist inclinations led China into an ultimately disastrous military adventure against China’s southern neighbour, Dai Viet (Vietnam, called Annam by the Chinese). In 1400 the young Tran dynasty, heir to the Dai Viet throne, had been deposed and a new dynasty proclaimed. From the beginning of Yongle’s reign Tran loyalist refugees urged him to intervene and restore legitimate rule, and, when his own envoys to Annam were murdered, in 1406, the emperor authorized a punitive campaign. Chinese forces rapidly occupied and pacified Annam. Because no Tran heir seemed available, the Yongle emperor in 1407 transformed Dai Viet from a tributary state into the new Chinese province of Annam. Local resistance broke out almost immediately and continued irrepressibly. Especially after 1418, guerrilla warfare against the Ming authorities made the Chinese position in Annam increasingly precarious. By that time the emperor had lost most of his early interest in the southern regions, and the situation was allowed to deteriorate until his grandson, the Xuande emperor, realistically, albeit with some humiliation, abandoned direct Ming rule of Annam in 1428.

# Yongle
During the early years of the Yongle emperor’s reign, the northern frontier, traditionally the zone of greatest danger to any Chinese regime, was relatively quiescent. At the outset of his Beijing-based insurrection in 1402, the Yongle emperor had sought and won the support of the Mongol tribes directly to his rear, in northeastern China. In later payment for this support, he in effect gave these Urianghad Mongols virtual autonomy by withdrawing China’s command posts south of the Great Wall, and he regularly sent the Urianghad chiefs substantial gifts. Other tribes beyond the northern frontier—the Eastern Mongols, or Tatars, and the Western Mongols, or Oyrats—were too disorganized to do more than struggle among themselves. In the far west, the Turko-Mongol empire builder Timur (Tamerlane) had already invaded and pillaged both India and Syria when the Yongle emperor came to the Chinese throne, and in 1404 Timur prepared to launch an expedition against China. Vaguely aware of this, the Yongle emperor alerted his commanders in the west to prepare for trouble; but Timur died in 1405, and the expedition was canceled. Thereafter, the emperor maintained amicable relations with Timur’s heirs at Samarkand and Herat, keeping the Central Asian trade routes open.
texts.7:
# Yongle
After his early years on the throne, the Yongle emperor’s attention was diverted from the south back to the northern frontier by the emergence of an effective new Tatar leader named Aruqtai. In 1410 the Yongle emperor resumed the aggressive extramural patrolling in the north that had preoccupied him as a prince in the 1380s and ’90s. Between 1410 and 1424 the emperor five times personally led grand armies northward into the Gobi, primarily against Aruqtai but occasionally against Oyrats or restless Urianghad groups. The campaigns culminated in only a few battles, in which the Chinese forces won indecisive victories, but they had the effect of forestalling the development of a new large-scale Mongol confederation that might have seriously threatened China. Astute diplomacy was also relied on during these years to keep the Mongols fragmented and to establish at least nominal Chinese authority over the Juchen (Chinese: Nüzchen, or Ruzhen) peoples in the far northeast, as distant as the Amur River (Chinese: Heilong Jiang).
texts.8:
# Yongle
## Transfer of the capital to Beijing
The most notable domestic event of the Yongle emperor’s reign was the transfer of the national capital and the central government from Nanjing to Beijing. This reflected and symbolized the emperor’s and the country’s shift of attention from the southern oceans to the northern land frontiers. Beijing was perhaps not the ideal site for the national capital: it historically had been associated primarily with “barbarian” dynasties such as the Yuan, it was far removed from China’s economic and cultural heartland, and it was dangerously close and exposed to the northern frontier. But it was the Yongle emperor’s personal power base, and it was a site from which the northern defenses could be kept under effective surveillance. In 1407 the emperor authorized transfer of the capital there, and from 1409 on he spent most of his time in the north. In 1417 large-scale work began on the reconstruction of Beijing, and thereafter the Yongle emperor never returned to Nanjing. The new Beijing palace was completed in 1420, and on New Year’s Day of 1421 Beijing formally became the national capital.

The future Hongwu emperor was born in 1328 as Zhu Chongba, a poor peasant of Haozhou (about 100 miles [160 km] northwest of Nanjing, near China’s east coast). Orphaned at 16, he became a monk at the Huangjue monastery near Fengyang to avoid starvation—a common practice for the sons of poor peasants. As a wandering mendicant, he often begged for food at Hefei (some 100 miles west of Nanjing) and surrounding areas, where no constituted authority existed. Indeed, all of central and northern China was suffering from drought and famine, and more than seven million people starved, a situation that encouraged the popular rebellions that started from around 1325. Led by plebeian bandits, the rebels attacked the rich, distributing their wealth and goods among the people.

## Foreign policy
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
By acknowledging their subordination to the Ming emperors, the Koreans were able to secure their northern border. This not only brought stability to the border, but also strengthened the legitimacy of the Korean government through official recognition from China. The ruling Joseon dynasty only came into power in 1392.[[169]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-193) The exchange of envoys, which had been frequent under previous emperors, continued during the Yongle Emperor's reign. The Yongle Emperor's first ambassadors arrived in Korea in 1402 to announce the new emperor's ascension. In the years that followed, there were regular contacts between the two countries, with the Koreans sending two to three delegations per year. Some of the Ming's demands were seen as excessive and difficult by the Koreans, but they still fulfilled them. These demands included providing horses and oxen for military purposes,[[xxv]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-194) bronze Buddha statues, relics, paper for printing Buddhist literature, and even sending girls to serve in the imperial harem.[[169]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-193) However, the Koreans maintained their autonomy in internal affairs.

## Foreign policy
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
During the Hongwu era, relations with the Ashikaga government of Japan were at a standstill. Hu Weiyong, who was executed in 1380, was accused of conspiring with Japanese assistance.[[170]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-195) However, in 1399, Shōgun Yoshimitsu took the initiative to restore contacts in order to make profit from trade with China.[[171]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-196) This led to another mission being sent in 1403, during which the Yongle Emperor's sovereignty was recognized. In the same year, the Ming government opened maritime trade offices in Ningbo, Quanzhou, and Guangzhou, which allowed Japanese merchants with government licenses to trade. However, in 1411, new Shōgun Yoshimochi implemented an isolationist policy and interrupted official relations. He also rejected the Ming's attempt to re-establish relations in 1417.[[170]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-195) Despite this, the allure of Chinese coins and goods was too strong for the Japanese to resist,[[171]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-196) and illegal private trade continued from the ports of southern Japan.[[170]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-195)

## Foreign policy
### Đại Việt
In the late 14th century, Đại Việt (present-day northern Vietnam) was facing internal weakness. In 1400, Lê Quý Ly overthrew the Trần dynasty and changed the name of the state to Đại Ngu. Despite pleas from Viet refugees to the Ming government to restore the fallen dynasty, the Yongle Emperor recognized the new Viet government and confirmed Lê Quý Ly's son as the ruler of Đại Ngu in the winter of 1403. However, relations between the two countries were strained due to escalating border disputes. Lê Quý Ly prepared for the impending conflict and continued to engage in border skirmishes. In the spring of 1406, his soldiers even ambushed a Ming diplomatic envoys accompanying the Trần pretender.[[172]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTETsai2002179-197) In response, the Yongle Emperor ordered an invasion. By late 1406, the Ming army had attacked Đại Ngu from two directions, quelling resistance by mid-1407. In July, the country was officially annexed to the Ming dynasty as Jiaozhi Province.[[173]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988230-198)

### Other Southeast Asian countries

In Southeast Asia, the Ming dynasty had a strong presence during the Yongle era. **The Fate of the Archives and Historical Source Issues**
According to the "Shuyu Zhouzilu" (written by Yan Congjian, completed in 1574), when the Chenghua Emperor (Xianzong) sought records of the Zheng He expeditions during the Chenghua era (1465–1487), the Ministry of War official Liu Daxia (1436–1516) is said to have stated: "The voyages of Sanbao to the Western Ocean wasted tens of thousands of money and grain, and the deaths of soldiers and civilians numbered in the tens of thousands. Even if rare treasures were brought back, what benefit is there to the state? This is truly a harmful policy, and one that ministers should earnestly remonstrate against."
It is also said that Liu Daxia hid or destroyed the archives, but this anecdote itself is a record from about 100 years after the event, and its accuracy as a historical fact is debated. Furthermore, recent research (Li Yingfa, 2014) has proposed the theory that what Liu Daxia hid or destroyed were the records of the Annam expedition, not the records of the Zheng He voyages.
In any case, since the "Zheng He Navigation Chart" contained in the "Wubeizhi" (compiled by Mao Yuanyi, 1621, published 1628) still exists, not all records were lost. This navigation chart records the route from Nanjing to the coast of East Africa and is considered academically important as the only surviving navigational record of the Zheng He expeditions.
**Maritime Expeditions from the Perspective of International Relations Theory**
**Hegemonic Stability Theory** provides one analytical framework. This theory allows for a view that sees Ming China as a regional hegemon that projected naval superiority to create a "Pax Sinica" (Chinese peace) or "pax Ming" (Ming peace) similar to the later "Pax Britannica" or "Pax Americana." According to this interpretation, the hegemonic order provided stability to the trade networks along the Indian Ocean coast.
texts.10:
However, there are dissenting views on this interpretation. Recent research has questioned whether the Ming dynasty functioned as the "stability provider" assumed by hegemonic stability theory. There is also a view that the Ming economy did not depend on maritime trade (most tax revenue came from agriculture) and that the expeditions were conducted to demonstrate power and status rather than to support the interests of Chinese merchants. The "pax Ming" discussed by Geoff Wade (2005) is also depicted as an "aggressive attempt at maritime dominance" rather than peaceful stability.
**Soft Power Projection** provides an alternative lens. An analysis by James R. Holmes and Toshi Yoshihara (2006) published in the U.S. Naval Institute's Proceedings describes the expeditions as "soft power at sea." The gifting of silk textiles, porcelain, and diplomatic recognition functioned through attraction rather than coercion. The tribute system provided participants with benefits such as protection, trading rights, and recognition of legitimacy. Holmes and Yoshihara argue that modern China is using Zheng He to build a "maritime diplomacy that confers legitimacy on China's naval ambitions and eases the concerns of coastal nations."
**The Cosmological View of Tianxia** provides an indigenous theoretical foundation. "Tianxia" (all under heaven) is a world order concept rooted in classical Chinese thought, based on the ideal of a "world without an outside" (wuwai). According to Zhao Tingyang (2021), this system rejects the binary opposition of friend and enemy and aims for an inclusive order that acknowledges differences without aiming for the annihilation of the other.
David Kang (2010) characterizes the tribute system as a combination of "hierarchy in form and flexibility in practice." China was positioned at the apex as the source of Confucian civilization, but in actual relationships, reciprocity and flexibility were observed. According to Kang, evidence that secondary states viewed this hierarchical order as legitimate can be found in the voluntary adoption of Confucian institutions and the mutual use of the tribute system.
Feng Zhang (2015) demonstrates that tribute diplomacy combined both "instrumental rationality" (maximization of self-interest) and "expressive rationality" (behavior based on Confucian sentiment and duty). Expressive rationality is a feature that has been little conceptualized in Western-centric international relations theory and was an essential component in the regional relations of the Ming dynasty.
texts.11:
**Academic Debate**
The academic debate over the nature of the Zheng He expeditions is not a simple binary opposition but can be classified into three main positions.
**The "Voyages of Friendship" interpretation** is mainly found in the official views of the Chinese government and academic literature within China. Premier Wen Jiabao (2004) stated that they "brought silk, tea, and Chinese culture, but did not occupy an inch of land," and Ambassador Guo Chongli characterized them as "voyages for friendship, not for resource plunder." This interpretation emphasizes the absence of permanent colonial bases and the lack of systematic exploitation.
**Proto-colonialist interpretations** are argued by Geoff Wade (Asia Research Institute, National University of Singapore, 2004/2005) and Charles Horner (Hudson Institute, 2009). Wade defines the expeditions as "maritime proto-colonialism," specifying it as "an early form of maritime colonialism in which a dominant maritime power, through force or the threat thereof, controlled key port cities in major East-West maritime trade networks." In "Rising China and Its Postmodern Fate," Horner argues that the Zheng He fleet engaged in "gunboat diplomacy" and was "exactly like other imperialist powers."
The grounds supporting this interpretation include the following:
texts.12:
*   **Military composition**: According to the "Veritable Records of the Ming" (Taizong Shilu), in a 1405 imperial decree, Zheng He was ordered to "lead 27,000 troops to the Western Ocean." Wade estimates that out of the 28,000 expedition personnel, approximately 26,000 were military personnel.

*   **Palembang attack (1407)**: Defeated the fleet of pirate Chen Zuyi, killing 5,000 people, and appointed Shi Jinqing as the "Pacification Commissioner of Old Port" (Jiugang Xuanweishi), establishing a Ming vassal state.

*   **Ceylon military intervention (1410-1411)**: Captured King Alakeshvara and escorted him to Nanjing, installing the pro-Ming Parakramabahu VI.

*   **Sumatra intervention (1415)**: Subdued and captured the usurper Sekandar, executing him in Nanjing.

*   **Malacca as a strategic base**: Constructed warehouses, granaries, and stockades, and in 1411, escorted King Parameswara and his 540-person entourage to China.
**Intermediate and power-projection interpretations** also exist. Edward Dreyer (2007) concluded that "a thorough examination of primary sources reveals that the purpose of the voyages was not mere exploration but in fact 'power projection'," clearly rejecting the "voyages of friendship" theory. Louise Levathes (1994), while describing it as an "age of exploration and conquest," presents a more complex picture, arguing that China "could have colonized but chose not to."
Note that caution is required with the term "vassal states." What the Ming dynasty established was a **tributary relationship**, where foreign monarchs acknowledged the superiority of the Emperor, performed the kowtow, and received investiture, but there was no permanent military garrisoning in the Western colonial sense. Tansen Sen proposes the term "Mingism" rather than "imperialism."

In the early years of his reign, he seems to have been fascinated by the regions beyond China’s southern borders, perhaps in part because of rumours that the Jianwen emperor had escaped overseas. In 1403 the Yongle emperor sent out three fleets under eunuch commanders to proclaim his accession throughout Southeast Asia as far as Java and southern India. More vigorously than any other ruler in Chinese history, he sought recognition from faraway potentates in these regions. Throughout his reign “tributary” missions regularly traveled to China from overseas, including local kings of Malacca and Brunei. Most renowned of the Yongle emperor’s many ocean admirals was the Muslim eunuch Zheng He, who led grand armadas on seven great voyages between 1405 and 1433. Zheng He visited no fewer than 37 countries, some as far away as the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, and the east coast of Africa almost as far south as Zanzibar, and from all the states that he visited Zheng He brought home envoys bearing tribute to acknowledge the Yongle emperor’s overlordship.

# Yongle
The emperor similarly sent a eunuch emissary on repeated tribute-seeking missions to Tibet and Nepal and a civil servant across Central Asia to Afghanistan and Russian Turkistan. The Yongle emperor became the only ruler in Chinese history to be acknowledged suzerain by the Japanese, under the Ashikaga shogun Yoshimitsu. For a short time the Japanese were so docile as to send their own subjects to the Chinese court for punishment as piratical plunderers of the Korean and Chinese coasts. But the succession of a new shogun brought about a less submissive attitude in Japan; from 1411 on, no tribute missions arrived from Japan despite the Yongle emperor’s inquiries, and Japanese raiders became active again on China’s coast. The emperor then threatened to send a punitive expedition against Japan if it would not reform. But in 1419, when the shogunate brusquely denied responsibility for any piratical activities and refused to resume the former tributary relationship, the Yongle emperor was too preoccupied with other matters to do more than grumble.
The Yongle emperor’s expansionist inclinations led China into an ultimately disastrous military adventure against China’s southern neighbour, Dai Viet (Vietnam, called Annam by the Chinese). In 1400 the young Tran dynasty, heir to the Dai Viet throne, had been deposed and a new dynasty proclaimed. From the beginning of Yongle’s reign Tran loyalist refugees urged him to intervene and restore legitimate rule, and, when his own envoys to Annam were murdered, in 1406, the emperor authorized a punitive campaign. Chinese forces rapidly occupied and pacified Annam. Because no Tran heir seemed available, the Yongle emperor in 1407 transformed Dai Viet from a tributary state into the new Chinese province of Annam. Local resistance broke out almost immediately and continued irrepressibly. Especially after 1418, guerrilla warfare against the Ming authorities made the Chinese position in Annam increasingly precarious. By that time the emperor had lost most of his early interest in the southern regions, and the situation was allowed to deteriorate until his grandson, the Xuande emperor, realistically, albeit with some humiliation, abandoned direct Ming rule of Annam in 1428.

# Yongle
During the early years of the Yongle emperor’s reign, the northern frontier, traditionally the zone of greatest danger to any Chinese regime, was relatively quiescent. At the outset of his Beijing-based insurrection in 1402, the Yongle emperor had sought and won the support of the Mongol tribes directly to his rear, in northeastern China. In later payment for this support, he in effect gave these Urianghad Mongols virtual autonomy by withdrawing China’s command posts south of the Great Wall, and he regularly sent the Urianghad chiefs substantial gifts. Other tribes beyond the northern frontier—the Eastern Mongols, or Tatars, and the Western Mongols, or Oyrats—were too disorganized to do more than struggle among themselves. In the far west, the Turko-Mongol empire builder Timur (Tamerlane) had already invaded and pillaged both India and Syria when the Yongle emperor came to the Chinese throne, and in 1404 Timur prepared to launch an expedition against China. Vaguely aware of this, the Yongle emperor alerted his commanders in the west to prepare for trouble; but Timur died in 1405, and the expedition was canceled. Thereafter, the emperor maintained amicable relations with Timur’s heirs at Samarkand and Herat, keeping the Central Asian trade routes open.

# Yongle
After his early years on the throne, the Yongle emperor’s attention was diverted from the south back to the northern frontier by the emergence of an effective new Tatar leader named Aruqtai. In 1410 the Yongle emperor resumed the aggressive extramural patrolling in the north that had preoccupied him as a prince in the 1380s and ’90s. Between 1410 and 1424 the emperor five times personally led grand armies northward into the Gobi, primarily against Aruqtai but occasionally against Oyrats or restless Urianghad groups. The campaigns culminated in only a few battles, in which the Chinese forces won indecisive victories, but they had the effect of forestalling the development of a new large-scale Mongol confederation that might have seriously threatened China. Astute diplomacy was also relied on during these years to keep the Mongols fragmented and to establish at least nominal Chinese authority over the Juchen (Chinese: Nüzchen, or Ruzhen) peoples in the far northeast, as distant as the Amur River (Chinese: Heilong Jiang).

## Transfer of the capital to Beijing
The most notable domestic event of the Yongle emperor’s reign was the transfer of the national capital and the central government from Nanjing to Beijing. This reflected and symbolized the emperor’s and the country’s shift of attention from the southern oceans to the northern land frontiers. Beijing was perhaps not the ideal site for the national capital: it historically had been associated primarily with “barbarian” dynasties such as the Yuan, it was far removed from China’s economic and cultural heartland, and it was dangerously close and exposed to the northern frontier. But it was the Yongle emperor’s personal power base, and it was a site from which the northern defenses could be kept under effective surveillance. In 1407 the emperor authorized transfer of the capital there, and from 1409 on he spent most of his time in the north. In 1417 large-scale work began on the reconstruction of Beijing, and thereafter the Yongle emperor never returned to Nanjing. The new Beijing palace was completed in 1420, and on New Year’s Day of 1421 Beijing formally became the national capital.

# Hongwu
**Hongwu** (born Oct. 21, 1328, Haozhou now Fengyang, [Anhui province], China—died June 24, 1398, Nanjing) was the Chinese emperor (reigned 1368–98) who founded the Ming dynasty that ruled China for nearly 300 years. During his reign, the Hongwu emperor instituted military, administrative, and educational reforms that centred power in the emperor.

# Hongwu
## Early life
The future Hongwu emperor was born in 1328 as Zhu Chongba, a poor peasant of Haozhou (about 100 miles [160 km] northwest of Nanjing, near China’s east coast). Orphaned at 16, he became a monk at the Huangjue monastery near Fengyang to avoid starvation—a common practice for the sons of poor peasants. As a wandering mendicant, he often begged for food at Hefei (some 100 miles west of Nanjing) and surrounding areas, where no constituted authority existed. Indeed, all of central and northern China was suffering from drought and famine, and more than seven million people starved, a situation that encouraged the popular rebellions that started from around 1325. Led by plebeian bandits, the rebels attacked the rich, distributing their wealth and goods among the people.

By acknowledging their subordination to the Ming emperors, the Koreans were able to secure their northern border. This not only brought stability to the border, but also strengthened the legitimacy of the Korean government through official recognition from China. The Yongle Emperor's first ambassadors arrived in Korea in 1402 to announce the new emperor's ascension. In the years that followed, there were regular contacts between the two countries, with the Koreans sending two to three delegations per year. Some of the Ming's demands were seen as excessive and difficult by the Koreans, but they still fulfilled them. These demands included providing horses and oxen for military purposes,[[xxv]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-194) bronze Buddha statues, relics, paper for printing Buddhist literature, and even sending girls to serve in the imperial harem.[[169]](https://www.marefa.org/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-193) However, the Koreans maintained their autonomy in internal affairs.

During the Hongwu era, relations with the Ashikaga government of Japan were at a standstill. Despite pleas from Viet refugees to the Ming government to restore the fallen dynasty, the Yongle Emperor recognized the new Viet government and confirmed Lê Quý Ly's son as the ruler of Đại Ngu in the winter of 1403.
